item.title: Tech news, 23 November 2026: Amazon and Decart, an open-weight Inkling 2 Mini, RTX Spark desktops and a ransomware claim against Nvidia
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: Amazon reportedly nears a deal for Decart to run AI on its own chips, Inkling 2 Mini ships open weights, RTX Spark desktops go on sale, Nvidia probes claim.
item.content:encoded:
Amazon is reported to be close to buying Decart, whose software helps AI models run on AWS's own chips. Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Mini with open weights sized for a laptop, and Nvidia's RTX Spark compact desktops went on sale for local AI work. Nvidia also said it is investigating a possible incident at a third-party partner after a ransomware group listed it.

Today's brief covers stories from 20 to 22 November.

1. Amazon reportedly nears a deal for Decart

Amazon is in advanced talks to buy Decart, a startup whose software helps AI models run across different chips including AWS's own Trainium, in a deal reported at about $7.5 billion that could be announced soon, according to reporting citing the Financial Times1. Nothing has been announced, and reports note Decart was valued at $4 billion earlier in the year2.

CTO take: the strategic point is software that makes non-Nvidia chips easier to use. If it works, AWS customers get more realistic alternatives for inference, and more price competition. Do not plan around a rumour, but do keep your serving stack portable: standard model formats, a serving layer you control and evaluation sets that let you compare accelerators on your own workloads. See LLM inference serving and inference architecture under memory constraints.

2. Thinking Machines releases Inkling 2 Mini with open weights

Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini under Apache 2.0, a looped mixture-of-experts model whose middle layers run several times per token, with a reported memory footprint of about 20 GB3. Coverage says it accepts text and images and is pitched to run on well-equipped laptops; benchmark claims come from the lab and independent testers and should be checked against your own tasks4.

CTO take: capable open-weight models that run on a developer's machine change two things: private experimentation without sending data out, and cheaper fallbacks for routine tasks. Add it to your evaluation set alongside your current models, and record its lineage in your model inventory, as in model provenance. Licence terms matter: check the acceptable use policy as well as the Apache licence.

3. RTX Spark compact desktops go on sale

Nvidia said compact desktops built on its RTX Spark platform are now available from ASUS, Dell and MSI, with machines from Acer, GIGABYTE, HP and a Microsoft developer box to follow5. The Next Web reports prices starting at $4,399, with configurations up to 128 GB of unified memory6.

CTO take: machines like this make local model work practical for small teams: prototyping, fine-tuning small models and running evaluations without cloud queues or data leaving the building. They are not production infrastructure. Treat them as developer workstations, with disk encryption, device management and clear rules on which data may sit on them. See my notes on an AI architect's desktop bench.

4. Nvidia investigates a possible partner incident after a ransomware claim

Nvidia said it is investigating an incident that may have affected a third-party partner, after the Gentlemen ransomware group listed the company on its leak site, and that it has found no indication its own systems or networks were affected7. The group had not published evidence at the time of reporting.

CTO take: "a partner may be affected" is now the most common shape of a large company's incident. If you share data with partners, know exactly what each one holds, set expectations for notification in contracts and be ready to answer customers before the facts are complete. See vendor access as perimeter.

What I'd do this week

  • Check how portable your model serving is across accelerators and clouds.
  • Add a capable small open-weight model to your evaluation set as a fallback candidate.
  • Set rules for local AI workstations: encryption, management and permitted data.
  • Review what data each partner holds and how quickly they must tell you about incidents.

I am a fractional CTO and AI architect based in India, the United States and the UAE, working globally. If any of these lands on your desk this week, analyse your challenge and bring the result to a call.

item.title: Do you know where your models come from? Model provenance after the House report on Chinese open-weight models
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A House report targets Chinese open-weight models and Cursor weighs dropping them. A CTO's take on model provenance: inventory, derivatives and the right to switch.
item.content:encoded:
Two House committees have recommended limiting Chinese open-weight models in federal work and creating a model provenance standard, and Cursor told them it would explore phasing such models out. Whatever you think of the politics, the question behind it is practical and global: can you say which models, and which models underneath them, power your products? Most companies cannot.

What happened

The House Select Committee on China and the House Homeland Security Committee published a joint report on Chinese open-weight models such as DeepSeek, Qwen and Kimi. It found that cost, customisation and near-frontier performance drive their adoption, and recommended restricting them in federal agencies and contract work, a national American open-weight model initiative and a model provenance standard1. Cursor told the committees it would explore phasing out Chinese-developed open-weight models because of geopolitical risk; CNBC reports its Composer coding model was built on a Moonshot Kimi model2.

The same week, India's Sarvam began offering hosted access to Chinese models including DeepSeek alongside its own, The Next Web reports, and the report itself warns that forcing companies off these models before trusted alternatives exist would raise costs3. The recommendations are not law. They are, however, a clear signal of the questions customers and regulators will start asking.

The real problem is hidden lineage

Cursor's case shows why this is harder than it looks. A product can be marketed under its own model name while being built on someone else's base model. Fine-tunes, distillations, merged models and hosted APIs all hide where the underlying weights came from. Software teams learned this with libraries: you depend not just on what you import but on everything it imports.

The CNCF's supply chain guidance describes exactly this structure for software, with direct and transitive dependencies each needing to be known and verified6. For models, the chain runs from base model to fine-tune to the hosted endpoint your product calls, and sometimes through a vendor that does not tell you.

What a useful model inventory records

Standards are starting to catch up. India's CERT-In expanded its bill of materials guidelines in 2025 to cover AI bills of materials alongside software, cryptographic and hardware ones4, and research such as AIBoMGen generates AI bills of materials during training, recording datasets, base model and configuration with signed attestations5. You do not need to wait for a final standard to keep a spreadsheet with the fields above.

Keep the right to switch

Provenance only helps if you can act on it. The architecture that makes switching cheap is the same one I recommend for cost and resilience: a model gateway between applications and models, evaluation sets for every important task, and at least one tested alternative for each.

SituationSensible stance
Selling to US federal agencies or their contractorsExpect origin questions now; prepare alternatives for affected uses
Regulated sectors such as finance and healthDocument lineage and evaluation; be ready to explain choices
Internal tools and experimentsRecord lineage; choose on quality, cost and data handling
Self-hosted open weightsOrigin matters less for data flow, more for licence and customer perception

Self-hosting an open-weight model keeps your data in your environment, whatever its origin. That is a different risk from sending data to a foreign API, and it deserves a different answer.

The CTO's take

This is not only an American question. Indian, European and Gulf customers ask their own versions, about sovereignty, data residency or licensing. The companies that handle it well will be the ones that already know what is inside their products and have kept the freedom to change it. That is an engineering discipline, not a political position. Related reading: per-market AI models, model routing, self-hosting open weights and evaluation sets.

item.title: One front door for research: securing lab-deployed AI tools at a Japanese university hospital
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a Japanese university hospital can find and secure lab-deployed AI research tools, after AI agents exploited a medical imaging zero-day on an exposed server.
item.content:encoded:
A Japanese university hospital ran research AI tools that individual labs had installed themselves: imaging annotation servers, notebook servers, model demos. Some were reachable from the internet, outside the hospital's security operations. When AI agents were reported to have found and exploited a zero-day in a medical imaging tool on exactly that kind of server, the goal became clear: find every research service, put it behind one front door, and do it without stopping the research.

The situation

A Japanese university hospital had a strong central IT function for clinical systems and a very different world in its research labs. Radiology, pathology and informatics groups ran their own AI tools: imaging annotation servers for labelling studies, notebook servers for model development, demo applications for collaborators. Some sat on lab machines, some on cloud accounts paid from research grants, and some were reachable from the internet so partners at other institutions could log in.

The hospital followed the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare's guidelines on the safety management of medical information systems, whose version 6.0 was restructured to respond to cyberattacks and wider cloud use, with separate volumes for governance, management and system operations3. Those controls were well applied to clinical systems. Research services were largely outside them.

Why now. In November 2026, Amazon reported that a suspected China-nexus operator used autonomous AI agents to map the API of MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging annotation tool, find a path traversal flaw and exploit it on university servers in East Asia1. The Register reported the agents went on to gain root2. The hospital's research groups used tools of exactly this kind. The board asked how many such servers were exposed. Nobody could answer.

What had to be true

  • Every research service known, with an owner, purpose and the data it can reach.
  • Nothing research-related directly reachable from the internet; one authenticated front door instead.
  • External collaborators still able to work, with their own identities, not shared passwords.
  • Patient data separated from experimental tools, with only de-identified data in research zones by default.
  • Research not stopped: labs keep the freedom to deploy, inside guard rails.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: central control without central bottlenecks

The easy answer, making central IT deploy every research tool, would have stopped research and pushed labs back to their own servers. The design had to separate who controls the front door from who controls each service. Kubernetes Gateway API is built around exactly that split: infrastructure providers define gateway classes, cluster operators run gateways, and application developers attach their own routes5.

In practice, the hospital's platform team ran the gateway and its authentication; each lab had a namespace and could publish routes to its own tools, which the gateway only accepted with an access policy attached. A new annotation server took the same steps for a lab as before, but could no longer appear on the internet without login.

The fastest win came before any platform work: an external scan of the hospital's address ranges and research cloud accounts. It turned an unknown into a list with owners.

Data was the second half. The ministry also publishes cyber security measures for medical institutions alongside the guidelines4, and the hospital extended the same thinking to research. Research tools received de-identified exports by default; identifiable data stayed in a separate zone that required approval and was never reachable from tools exposed to external collaborators. The pattern follows the health evidence platform and federated health analytics, and the gateway approach builds on moving to Gateway API.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
One authenticated gateway for all research toolsSecure each tool individuallyTools vary too much; the front door is the control point
Labs own their routesCentral IT deploys everythingKeeps research moving; avoids new shadow servers
Federated identities for collaboratorsShared accounts and passwordsAccess tied to a person and revocable
De-identified data by defaultIdentifiable data where convenientLimits harm if a research tool is compromised
Retire what has no ownerLeave running until someone complainsUnowned services are never patched

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: start with an external scan and a service register; it changed the conversation from fear to a list. Differently: bring lab leads in as co-designers of the platform from the first week. Researchers adopted it fastest where they had shaped the deployment templates. See AI-assisted intrusions and the tech news for 22 November.

item.title: Tech news, 22 November 2026: AI agents exploit a MONAI Label zero-day, an Entra flaw, a House report on Chinese open-weight models and Signal versus OS assistants
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: AI agents found and exploited a medical imaging zero-day, an Entra Connect Health flaw exposed tenant data, a House report on Chinese models, Signal vs AI.
item.content:encoded:
Amazon reported that a China-linked operator's autonomous AI agents found and exploited a zero-day in an open-source medical imaging tool. Microsoft disclosed that a flaw in Entra Connect Health let attackers read tenant metadata including administrator emails. Two House committees recommended limits on Chinese open-weight models, and Signal began blocking operating system AI assistants from reading chats.

Today's brief covers stories from 20 to 21 November.

1. AI agents find and exploit a medical imaging zero-day

Amazon Threat Intelligence reported that a suspected China-nexus operator used autonomous agents from the open-source Cairn framework to map the API of MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging annotation tool, find a path traversal flaw in a file upload function and exploit it against university servers in East Asia1. The Register reports the agents went on to gain root by planting a Python start-up hook, and that Amazon found the campaign because the attackers left their agent instance publicly reachable2.

CTO take: this case stands out because the agents found a new flaw rather than only chaining known ones, and the target is telling: a research tool deployed by a lab, exposed to the internet, outside normal IT oversight. Hospitals, universities and health-tech companies should find every research and annotation server that is internet-facing and put it behind authentication and a VPN. Note the escalation route too: the same Python start-up hook technique as the agent-framework compromise. See AI-assisted intrusions.

2. An Entra Connect Health flaw exposes tenant metadata

Microsoft disclosed that attackers exploited an API flaw in Entra Connect Health to read tenant-level metadata, including administrator email addresses and tenant configuration; it fixed the flaw on 19 November, is notifying affected customers and published a read-only script so administrators can see what may have been exposed3. Reports say passwords, hashes and tokens were not exposed.

CTO take: leaked administrator emails plus tenant details are a ready-made target list for phishing and impersonation, so the risk outlives the fix. Check Azure Service Health for a notice, run Microsoft's script, warn your administrators specifically, and confirm every admin account uses phishing-resistant sign-in. Consider separate, unpublished addresses for administrator accounts. See the access hardening case study.

3. House committees recommend limits on Chinese open-weight models

Two House committees published a joint report on Chinese open-weight models such as DeepSeek, Qwen and Kimi, recommending restrictions on their use in federal agencies and contract work, a national American open-weight model initiative and a model provenance standard4. CNBC reports Cursor told the committees it would explore phasing out Chinese-developed open-weight models because of geopolitical risk5.

CTO take: recommendations are not rules, but US companies that sell to government, or to customers who do, should expect questions about where their models come from. Know which models, including fine-tunes and distilled derivatives, sit inside your products and tools, and keep an abstraction that lets you switch. That is good practice regardless of politics. See per-market AI models, model routing and my US page.

4. Signal blocks operating system AI assistants from reading chats

Signal now blocks screenshots and screen recording by default on supported iPhones and uses its screen security feature on Android, to stop Apple's and Google's AI assistants from reading chats on screen; it says it cannot do the same on macOS and has asked platform makers for a proper way to keep AI agents out of sensitive apps6.

CTO take: operating system assistants that read the screen are a new data path for every app that shows sensitive information: banking, health, internal tools. Product teams should check what their apps expose to screen-reading assistants, use the platform flags available for sensitive screens, and update privacy notices. Security teams should add OS assistants to their data flow maps. See on-device data and consent.

What I'd do this week

  • Find internet-facing research and annotation servers and put them behind authentication.
  • Run Microsoft's Entra Connect Health script and brief administrators about targeted phishing.
  • List every model, including derivatives, in your products and tools, with its origin.
  • Check which sensitive screens in your apps are visible to OS AI assistants.

I am a fractional CTO and AI architect based in India, the United States and the UAE, working globally. If any of these lands on your desk this week, analyse your challenge and bring the result to a call.

item.title: AI-assisted intrusions are here: what the ARTEX warning changes for defenders
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: The FBI warns an AI pentesting framework is powering real intrusions, and the European Commission confirms an AI-assisted attack. A CTO's take on what to change now.
item.content:encoded:
In one week, the FBI warned that an autonomous AI penetration testing framework is being used in real intrusions, some reaching privileged access in under three hours, and the European Commission confirmed that an AI-assisted attack disrupted its staff systems. The techniques are not new. The speed, persistence and cost are. That changes which defences matter most.

What was reported

On 13 November the FBI issued a FLASH warning about ARTEX, an autonomous penetration testing framework that uses AI agents connected to external language models to plan and chain attack techniques1. The FBI says it is being used in real intrusions, and that some went from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours2. Reporting says the tool was published openly, later withdrawn, and remains available through forks and a commercial edition, and that attackers favour cheap models that do not refuse requests framed as penetration testing5. Targets span sectors including energy, manufacturing and telecoms3.

Days later, the European Commission confirmed that an AI-assisted cyberattack detected in October disrupted staff systems including HR, medical reimbursement and translation services, some for more than ten days4. Press reports link that campaign to the same framework; the Commission has not confirmed it.

What actually changes

Nothing in the reporting describes a new class of vulnerability. An AI agent running a penetration testing framework uses the same techniques a human tester would. Three things change, and each shifts which defences matter.

The cost point matters most for mid-sized companies. Attacks that used to need skilled people were reserved for valuable targets. When an agent can do the reconnaissance and chaining for the price of model calls, the threshold drops, and organisations that relied on not being interesting lose that protection.

Defences that work at machine speed

If an attacker can chain techniques in hours, a defence that depends on a person noticing an alert the next morning is too slow. The controls that hold up are the ones that sit in the path of every request and decide automatically. Kubernetes admission control is a good model: every API request passes authentication, authorisation, then mutating and validating checks before anything changes6. The same idea applies across an estate: put the decision where the action happens.

ControlWhy it matters more now
Shrink what is exposedAn agent will find every internet-facing service; fewer services means fewer chances
Phishing-resistant sign-in for staff and adminsCredential theft remains the cheapest first step to automate
Patch exposed systems in daysExploits for published flaws are chained faster than monthly cycles allow
Segment management planesA foothold should not reach identity, virtualisation or backups directly
Automated containmentDisable accounts and isolate hosts on high-confidence signals without waiting for a person
Short-lived credentialsStolen tokens should expire before an agent finishes using them

The test: if an attacker got a foothold at 2am on a Saturday, what stops them reaching an administrator account before Monday? If the answer is a person reading alerts, that is the gap.

Use the same tools on yourself

The uncomfortable corollary is that defenders can use these frameworks too. Running an autonomous testing tool against your own external surface, with permission and in a controlled scope, shows what an attacker's agent would find, faster than an annual penetration test. The governance matters: a defined scope, approved models, logging of every action and a kill switch. The same controls I describe for production agents in prompt injection defences and agent sandboxing apply to security agents.

The CTO's take

AI-assisted attacks are less a new threat than a price cut on old ones. The organisations most affected will be the ones that relied on being too small or too obscure to bother with, and the ones whose response depends on business hours. The fixes are familiar and unglamorous: expose less, authenticate strongly, patch the edge quickly and let systems contain obvious compromise automatically. This month's incidents, from vendor admin tools to the vCenter campaign, show where to start. For regulated firms, the AI cyber risk controls case study shows how this maps to supervisory expectations.

item.title: Fast, lawful and reviewable: creditworthiness assessment at checkout for an EU buy now, pay later provider
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How an EU buy now, pay later provider can meet the revised Consumer Credit Directive: checkout-speed creditworthiness assessment, permitted data only and human review.
item.content:encoded:
A buy now, pay later provider operating in several EU countries approved purchases at checkout with a light-touch risk check. The revised Consumer Credit Directive brings that kind of credit into scope from 20 November 2026, with a proper creditworthiness assessment, limits on the data that may be used and a right to human review of automated decisions. The goal was to meet all three without making checkout slow.

The situation

A buy now, pay later provider operated in several EU countries, approving split payments at online checkouts. Its risk check was built for speed and fraud: device signals, basket details, repayment history with the provider and a fraud model. It was not designed as a creditworthiness assessment, and it used whatever data improved the model.

The revised Consumer Credit Directive changes that. Member States had to apply it from 20 November 20261, and it brings much buy now, pay later lending into scope as regulated consumer credit2. That means a creditworthiness assessment based on relevant information, limits on what personal data may be used, and, where the assessment involves automated processing, a right for the consumer to obtain human intervention, an explanation and a review13.

Why now. The rules applied from 20 November 2026, while several large markets were still finishing their national laws2. The provider needed one platform that met the directive everywhere it operated and could absorb national differences as each country's law settled4.

What had to be true

  • A real creditworthiness assessment for every in-scope agreement, not a relabelled fraud score.
  • Only permitted data in decisions, enforced by the platform, not by convention.
  • Checkout stays fast: the decision has to fit inside the merchant's payment flow.
  • Every automated decision reviewable: what was used, which rules and model, and why.
  • National differences as configuration, because each country's law arrived on its own timetable.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: keeping prohibited data out of decisions, and out of logs

The old model had learned from everything available. Some of those signals were reasonable for fraud but inappropriate for creditworthiness, and some could stand in for categories of data the rules exclude. The fix was to tag every feature in the feature store with where it may be used: fraud only, credit permitted, or not used, per country. The decision service could only request credit features from the permitted set, so a model trained on something else simply could not be deployed for credit.

Logs were the second leak. Request headers and payloads carried details that should never reach a credit decision or a debugging tool. The team set telemetry to exclude by default and include only what was needed, masking sensitive values. OpenTelemetry's eBPF instrumentation shows the pattern, with a default exclude policy and an obfuscation value for headers that must be visible but not readable5.

Data restrictions only work if they are enforced where features are served. A policy document cannot stop a data scientist from adding a column; a permission on the feature can.

The decision record and review workbench reused the approach from the explainable credit decisions case study, with one difference: here the record had to be written within the checkout budget, so it was designed as a single append to a fast store with asynchronous enrichment afterwards. Idempotency followed idempotent payment pipelines, so retries from merchants never produced two decisions.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Separate fraud and credit stepsOne combined risk scoreDifferent purposes justify different data
Permissions on featuresData policy documentsEnforced at the point of use
Retrain on permitted data onlyKeep the old model and filter inputsA model can rely on proxies for removed data
Write the record before respondingLog asynchronouslyNo decision exists without its evidence
Countries as configurationCode branches per marketNational laws arrived at different times
Telemetry excludes by defaultCapture everything, redact laterSensitive data never lands in tools

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: treat the permitted data list as a product owned jointly by credit risk and engineering, enforced in the feature store. Differently: involve the review team before building the workbench. They knew which context they needed to decide quickly and fairly, and the first version showed too much detail in the wrong order. See structured outputs for how explanations were generated consistently and the EU AI Act roadmap for the high-risk credit scoring rules that come later.

item.title: Tech news, 21 November 2026: the European Commission's AI-assisted attack, how the vCenter campaign began, a TfL breach and Anthropic's Texas data centre
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: the European Commission confirms an AI-assisted cyberattack, vCenter attacks are traced to a BeyondTrust zero-day, TfL is breached, Anthropic's Texas lease.
item.content:encoded:
The European Commission confirmed that an AI-assisted cyberattack disrupted staff services for days. Google's researchers traced the vCenter zero-day campaign to a China-linked group that first broke in through a BeyondTrust remote support flaw. Transport for London disclosed a breach of Oyster photocard accounts, and a filing named Anthropic as the tenant of a large Texas data centre lease.

Today's brief covers stories from 19 to 20 November.

1. The European Commission confirms an AI-assisted cyberattack

The European Commission confirmed that an AI-assisted cyberattack, detected on 22 October, disrupted staff services including its HR platform Sysper, the MyPMO medical reimbursement system and translation services, with some outages lasting more than ten days1. The Commission says it has found no evidence of a data breach so far and that the investigation continues; press reports link the campaign to a publicly available AI penetration testing framework, which the Commission has not confirmed2.

CTO take: the practical change from AI-assisted attacks is speed and persistence, not new techniques. Attackers can try more paths, faster, against everything you expose. That makes the basics more urgent: phishing-resistant sign-in, quick patching of internet-facing systems, segmentation so one compromised service does not reach the rest, and detection tuned to spot rapid, automated reconnaissance. European public bodies and their suppliers should expect questions on exactly these controls. See the AI cyber risk controls case study and my Europe page.

2. The vCenter zero-day campaign began with a BeyondTrust flaw

Google's Mandiant and Threat Intelligence Group attribute exploitation of the vCenter authentication bypass to Armory Castle, a suspected China-nexus espionage group, which first compromised BeyondTrust Remote Support instances through a separate zero-day in late August, then moved to an internal appliance and on to vCenter from early September3. Google says a small number of organisations are confirmed compromised and others are likely affected4.

CTO take: this is the pattern from this month's vendor admin access analysis playing out: a remote access tool at the edge, then the virtualisation control plane. If you run BeyondTrust Remote Support or vCenter, patch both, then hunt rather than assume: look for new administrator and single sign-on accounts, unusual vCenter logins and unexpected outbound traffic from management appliances since late August. Keep management interfaces on networks that remote support tools cannot reach directly.

3. Transport for London discloses an Oyster photocard breach

Transport for London said about 265,000 Oyster photocard customers were affected after it detected suspicious activity on 16 November and took the photocard system offline; reported exposed data includes names, contact details, addresses and security questions and answers5. TfL says passwords and payment card details were not compromised, and customers will be asked to reset passwords and security answers when the portal returns6.

CTO take: security questions are the weak point here. Once their answers leak, they are useful to attackers on every other service that uses the same questions, and customers cannot change their mother's maiden name. If your product still uses knowledge-based questions for recovery, replace them with stronger recovery factors. UK organisations should also note how quickly the regulator was informed. See the access hardening case study and my UK page.

4. A filing names Anthropic as tenant of a $28 billion Texas lease

Riot Platforms had disclosed a 15-year lease of its Corsicana, Texas campus to a frontier AI lab, with total contract value of about $28 billion7. Its latest quarterly filing names Anthropic as the tenant8.

CTO take: long leases like this are how AI providers secure future capacity, and they are a useful signal for customers. A provider that has locked in power and space is better placed to honour capacity commitments, but also carries fixed costs that shape its pricing. When negotiating, ask providers about capacity guarantees and regions, not just per-token prices. See AI capacity contracts and the multi-region AI capacity case study.

What I'd do this week

  • Patch BeyondTrust Remote Support and vCenter, then hunt for new admin and SSO accounts since late August.
  • Check that management interfaces are unreachable from remote support and user networks.
  • Replace security questions in account recovery with stronger factors.
  • Review detection for fast, automated reconnaissance against internet-facing services.
  • Ask AI providers about capacity guarantees in your regions at the next renewal.

I am a fractional CTO and AI architect based in India, the United States and the UAE, working globally. If any of these lands on your desk this week, analyse your challenge and bring the result to a call.

item.title: Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter: how to choose a Kubernetes node autoscaler
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Cluster Autoscaler scales node groups; Karpenter provisions nodes to fit pods. A comparison of how each works, what managed versions change and how to choose.
item.content:encoded:
Node autoscaling decides how much you pay for Kubernetes and how fast new work starts. Kubernetes now sponsors two autoscalers with different models: Cluster Autoscaler, which grows and shrinks node groups you define, and Karpenter, which picks and launches nodes to fit the pods waiting. Cloud providers increasingly run Karpenter for you. Here is how they differ, and how I decide.

Two models of node autoscaling

The Kubernetes documentation describes node autoscaling as provisioning nodes when pods cannot be scheduled and consolidating them when they are underused, and lists two autoscalers sponsored by SIG Autoscaling: Cluster Autoscaler and Karpenter1. They solve the same problem from opposite ends.

Cluster Autoscaler works with node groups you define in advance: a group of one machine type, another for GPUs, perhaps a Spot group. When pods are pending, it grows the group whose nodes would fit them; when nodes are underused, it shrinks groups. Your choices about machine types are made up front, in the groups.

Karpenter starts from the pods. It reads what pending pods need, chooses machines to fit them within the limits you set in NodePools, launches them directly and manages their whole lifecycle, including replacing and consolidating them later1. Your choices are expressed as constraints rather than fixed groups.

How a scale-up differs

The practical consequence is flexibility. With Cluster Autoscaler, a workload that needs an unusual shape needs a node group that already offers it. With Karpenter, it needs a NodePool whose constraints allow it. That is why Karpenter tends to suit mixed and changing workloads, and why it needs firmer guard rails: a loose NodePool can launch machine types you never tested.

Scale-down is where the real difference is

Scale-up gets the attention, but cost is decided on the way down. Karpenter's disruption controls cover consolidation, which removes or replaces underused nodes with cheaper ones, as well as drift, when a node no longer matches its configuration, and expiry after a set lifetime2. Disruption budgets limit how many nodes can be disrupted at once and can be scheduled, so you can, for example, allow consolidation only outside business hours4.

That power has a cost: pods get moved more often. Workloads without pod disruption budgets, with long start-up times or with local state will feel it. The Headlamp plugin for Karpenter surfaces these scaling and disruption decisions in a UI6, and the view below shows the other side: a node whose disruption was blocked, which is what you want for a protected workload and what you need to notice when it stops consolidation entirely.

Managed options change the question

You may not have to run either yourself. AKS node auto-provisioning provisions and manages virtual machines in response to pending pods using Karpenter, configured through NodePools and AKS-specific node classes3. EKS Auto Mode manages compute for you and replaces nodes after a maximum lifetime of 21 days, which you can shorten5.

Managed versions remove the work of running the autoscaler, but they also make choices for you: node images, lifetimes and which settings you can change. Read the limitations pages before committing, especially if you need particular operating systems, network modes or access to nodes.

Side by side

QuestionCluster AutoscalerKarpenter
What you defineNode groups with fixed machine typesNodePools with constraints and limits
Scale-up decisionWhich group to growWhich machines to launch
Scale-downRemove underused nodes from groupsConsolidate, replace, handle drift and expiry
PredictabilityHigh: only the shapes you listedDepends on how tight your constraints are
Workload churnLowerHigher unless budgets are tuned
Best fitStable fleets, pinned GPU pools, platforms without a Karpenter providerMixed or bursty workloads, Spot, cost-sensitive fleets

How I decide

If your workloads cannot tolerate being moved, Karpenter's main advantage turns into a source of incidents. Fix disruption tolerance first, then change autoscaler.

For AI workloads, I often run both patterns: Karpenter for general and bursty services, and pinned, separately managed GPU capacity where warm nodes and scarce accelerators matter more than consolidation. See GPU scheduling with DRA, scale to zero, AI cost allocation and the Kubernetes FinOps case study.

item.title: Agents inside, attackers outside: AI cyber risk controls for a UK payments firm
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a UK payments firm can govern its own AI agents and defend against AI-enabled attacks, in line with new Bank of England, PRA and FCA practices on AI cyber risk.
item.content:encoded:
A UK payments firm had AI agents in customer support, fraud operations and engineering, each built differently and each with its own access. At the same time, attacks on it were getting faster and more convincing. The goal was one way to build and govern agents, and controls that assume attackers use AI too, in a form the firm could show its regulators.

The situation

A UK payments and e-money firm had adopted AI quickly and unevenly. Customer support used an agent that could look up transactions and raise refunds. Fraud operations used one that summarised alerts and suggested account restrictions. Engineering used coding agents with access to repositories and deployment pipelines. Each was built by a different team, on a different framework, with its own service accounts and its own idea of logging.

At the same time, the attacks the firm saw were changing: more convincing phishing, impersonation of executives in calls and messages asking for urgent payment changes, and faster exploitation of newly published flaws. The firm already worked to the FCA's operational resilience rules, which require important business services to be identified and kept within impact tolerances3.

Why now. In November 2026 the Bank of England, PRA and FCA published a consultation on cyber risk and resilience management, CP17/26 and GC26/9, clarifying how firms should meet existing requirements, with responses due by 26 February 20272. Alongside it they published effective practices on AI-related cyber risk, which treat AI as creating new risks, amplifying existing ones and helping defenders, and which include reducing the attack surface against AI-enabled attacks1. The board wanted to know how the firm compared, before a supervisor asked.

What had to be true

  • Every agent known: owner, purpose, model, tools and data it can reach.
  • One way to build agents, so controls are written once.
  • Agent actions as accountable as staff actions: identity, least privilege, logs and a way to stop them.
  • Defences that assume attackers use AI, especially for payments and access changes.
  • Everything tied to important business services, so AI risk fits the resilience framework the firm already runs.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: controlling agents the firm did not build the same way

The three agent estates could not be governed one by one; there was no shared place to put a control. The answer was to move them onto one framework over time, so identity, tool access, logging and a kill switch were properties of the platform rather than of each team's code. OpenTelemetry's work on agent observability draws the same distinction between agent applications and the frameworks they are built on, and argues for standard telemetry at the framework level so every application inherits it5.

The fastest risk reduction came before any migration: an inventory, then removing tools agents did not need. Some had write access they had never used.

The second half of the hard part was outside the firm. Impersonation attacks target the same processes agents touch: refunds, payee changes, admin access. Those changes now need a person to approve them through a separate, verified channel, never on the strength of a message, call or agent request alone. The pattern follows the deepfake-resistant onboarding and staff access hardening case studies, and the agent platform builds on the enterprise MCP agent platform.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
One agent framework for the firmEach team chooses its ownControls built once and applied everywhere
All tool calls through a gatewayAgents call APIs directlyOne place to scope, log and revoke access
Per-agent, short-lived identitiesShared service accountsActions traceable to an agent; stolen tokens expire
Human approval for money and access changesTrust agent or message aloneImpersonation and injection target exactly these steps
Map to existing resilience frameworkA separate AI risk registerAI risk sits where the board already looks

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: start with the inventory and the tool gateway, which reduced risk before any larger change, and treat the regulators' effective practices as a checklist rather than waiting for final guidance. Differently: involve the contact centre and finance teams from day one. The impersonation attempts reached them first, and their ideas made the approval steps practical. The NCSC's Cyber Assessment Framework, which the consultation aligns with4, was a useful common language between engineering and risk. item.title: Tech news, 20 November 2026: a critical vCenter bypass, Malaysia and US chip rules, UK AI cyber practices and Anthropic's market debut
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: a critical vCenter authentication bypass, Malaysia tells data centres to follow US chip rules, UK regulators set AI cyber practices, Anthropic lists.
item.content:encoded:
Broadcom patched a critical authentication bypass in VMware vCenter, with reports that it was exploited before the fix. Malaysia told its data centre operators to comply with the new US rules on advanced chips as Washington offered support for a Malaysian sovereign AI cloud. UK financial regulators published effective practices for AI-related cyber risk, and Anthropic's shares began trading on Nasdaq.

Today's brief covers stories from 18 to 19 November.

1. Broadcom patches a critical vCenter authentication bypass

Broadcom's advisory VMSA-2026-0009 fixes five flaws across vCenter, SDDC Manager and VMware Tools, the most serious being CVE-2026-123890, a 9.8-rated authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service that lets an unauthenticated attacker with network access to vCenter gain access; there is no workaround1. BleepingComputer reports the flaw was exploited as a zero-day since September by China-linked attackers2; Broadcom's advisory itself is reported not to describe exploitation, so treat that as reported rather than confirmed by the vendor.

CTO take: vCenter is the control plane for every virtual machine it manages, so this is a patch-tonight item for anyone running it. Patch, then check: review vCenter authentication and administrative activity since September, and confirm vCenter is reachable only from a management network, never from user networks or the internet. If you are still on a version without a public fix, that is the moment to fund the upgrade. See admin tools as perimeter and the management plane hardening case study.

2. Malaysia tells data centres to follow US chip rules, as the US backs its sovereign AI cloud

The US rule on remote access to advanced semiconductors was published in the Federal Register on 19 November3. Malaysia's trade minister said data centre operators must comply, including licences for advanced chips, and that the government would notify approved data centre projects and seek clarification from the US on licensing and third-party services4. Separately, Bloomberg reports the US will offer $50 million to support Malaysia's sovereign AI cloud5.

CTO take: for anyone buying GPU capacity in Malaysia, the practical effect is more know-your-customer questions from providers and some uncertainty about how third-party cloud services will be licensed. Keep your ownership and end-use information ready, avoid single-provider dependence in the region while the detail settles, and check contract terms for what happens if a provider loses a licence. See the Malaysia GPU cloud case study and my Southeast Asia page.

3. UK financial regulators publish AI cyber risk practices

The Bank of England, PRA and FCA published a consultation on cyber risk and resilience management, CP17/26 and GC26/9, which clarifies how firms should meet existing requirements and is open until 26 February 20277. Alongside it, a separate effective practices paper sets out how firms and financial market infrastructures are managing cyber risk related to AI, including reducing their attack surface against AI-enabled attacks6.

CTO take: effective practices are not rules, but they become the benchmark supervisors use in conversations. UK banks, insurers and payment firms should map their AI use, including agents and third-party models, against the practices now, and respond to the consultation if the expectations do not fit how they actually operate. Firms outside the UK can use it as a free, well-reasoned checklist. See the UK cyber resilience case study and my UK page.

4. Anthropic's shares begin trading

Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share, raising more than $81 billion in the largest offering on record8. Its shares opened on Nasdaq on 19 November at $111.50, TechRepublic reports9, and later closed lower than that opening price.

CTO take: for customers, a listed AI supplier means more public disclosure about capacity, costs and risks, which is useful in vendor reviews, and more pressure on revenue, which can show up in pricing and packaging. Neither changes the basic advice: keep a model gateway so you can switch providers, and track each provider's terms as carefully as their benchmarks. See LLM model routing and the AI provider resilience case study.

What I'd do this week

  • Patch vCenter, restrict access to a management network and review activity since September.
  • If you use GPU capacity in Malaysia, ask providers how the US licensing affects your service and contract.
  • UK financial firms: compare AI and agent use against the new effective practices and plan a consultation response.
  • Check that you could move your main AI workloads to a second provider without a rewrite.

item.title: The agent-framework hack: why installing a package was enough to lose your cloud secrets
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Poisoned agent-framework releases stole cloud and CI secrets at Python start-up. A CTO's take on .pth hooks, why agent tooling is a prime target and what to change in CI.
item.content:encoded:
Two releases of Microsoft's agent-framework package on PyPI carried a credential stealer that ran every time Python started, whether or not anyone imported the package. The mechanism is an old, documented Python feature. The target was the place where agent tooling now lives: developer laptops and CI runners full of cloud credentials. Here is what happened, why it worked, and what to change.

What happened

On 17 November, versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 of agent-framework, Microsoft's Python package for building AI agents, were published to PyPI with a credential stealer targeting Azure, Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions secrets1. Both have been removed, and Microsoft has said it is investigating2. Wiz identifies 1.26.0 as the latest safe version3.

Two details matter more than the headline. The releases appeared under the legitimate publisher rather than a lookalike name, and JFrog reports the attacker repacked the clean release rather than compromising Microsoft's build, which points to stolen publishing credentials4. And the two malicious versions went out within about half an hour of each other, the second moving the payload to a new file5. Anyone whose tooling upgraded automatically in that window got it.

Why installing was enough

The payload was delivered through a .pth file. Python's site module processes these path configuration files at start-up, and executes any line that begins with import6. It is a documented feature meant for setting up paths. It also means any installed package can run code every time Python starts, in every script, test run and notebook in that environment, without ever being imported4.

That changes the usual reasoning about risk. Teams often assume a dependency is only dangerous on the code paths that call it. Start-up hooks, install scripts and build plugins break that assumption: the risk is in the environment, not the call graph.

Why agent tooling is the target

Agent frameworks are installed where the valuable credentials are. Developers run them on laptops signed in to cloud consoles; CI pipelines run their tests with deployment credentials loaded; agents themselves are often given broad tokens so they can call tools. A package that sits in those environments is worth more to an attacker than almost any library in production, where secrets are usually narrower and better managed.

They are also young, fast-moving and upgraded eagerly. Teams building with agents want the newest release, so loose version ranges and automatic updates are common. That is exactly the window this attack used.

What to change in CI and developer environments

The CNCF's software supply chain paper treats build infrastructure as needing the same security as the production it builds for, and recommends single-use build workers so a compromise cannot persist or spread across builds7. Most of the fixes here follow from taking that seriously.

ControlWhat it stopsCost
Lockfiles with hashes for every installSilently picking up a new releaseLow; needs a routine for updates
A cooling-off period before new releases are allowedInstalling a release in its first hours, when most poisoned versions are caughtLow; small delay on fixes
Separate install and secret-holding steps in CIStart-up hooks reading deployment credentials during testsMedium; pipeline changes
Short-lived, narrowly scoped CI credentialsStolen secrets being useful for long or broadlyMedium; identity federation work
Single-use build workersA compromise persisting across buildsMedium; often already available
Internal package mirror with policyUnreviewed packages reaching any environmentHigher; worth it at scale

The most effective single change is keeping deployment credentials out of any step that installs or runs third-party code. Tests do not need the keys to production.

For developers, the equivalent is not running agent experiments in the same environment, or with the same signed-in cloud session, as production administration. A disposable container or virtual environment with no standing credentials costs little and limits what a poisoned package can find.

If you installed an affected version

  • Find it: search lockfiles, CI logs and package caches for agent-framework 1.26.1 or 1.26.2.
  • Assume every credential reachable from those machines and runners is exposed, not just Azure and GitHub; reports describe the stealer reading environment variables and local configuration more broadly2.
  • Rotate first, then investigate: review cloud audit logs and CI histories for use of those credentials since 17 November.
  • Rebuild affected environments rather than cleaning them, and pin to a verified version.

The CTO's take

This is the same lesson as the recent vendor access incidents, one layer down: trust granted for convenience becomes access for attackers. Package registries are run by the publishers you depend on, and their credentials can be stolen like anyone's. The defence is to assume a dependency will eventually be poisoned and design so that, when it happens, it finds nothing worth taking. item.title: A query, not a hunt: building a live software inventory for an Indian stockbroker after Java4Shell
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How an Indian stockbroker can turn SEBI's SBOM requirement into a live runtime inventory, so the next Java4Shell is a query and a rebuild, not a week-long hunt.
item.content:encoded:
An Indian stockbroker ran its trading, identity and back-office systems on Java, some built in-house and some bought. When Java4Shell was disclosed, nobody could say quickly where every Java runtime was or which version it ran. The SBOMs produced for SEBI's cyber framework listed libraries, not runtimes. The goal was an inventory that answers that question in minutes, and a patch path that rebuilds rather than repairs.

The situation

A mid-sized Indian stockbroker ran most of its estate on Java: an in-house order management service, a customer portal, Keycloak for identity, Jenkins for builds, and several bought products for exchange connectivity, risk and back office, each shipping with its own Java. Some ran in Kubernetes, some on virtual machines, and a few on servers that only the vendor touched.

Under SEBI's Cybersecurity and Cyber Resilience Framework, the firm already produced software bills of materials for software supporting core operations, as regulated entities are expected to, covering in-house, third-party, open-source and SaaS software3. CERT-In's guidelines set out what those SBOMs should contain and have since been extended to other kinds of bill of materials4. On paper, the firm was well placed.

Why now. Java4Shell, a flaw in the Base64 decoder of OpenJDK's runtime, was disclosed in November 2026, with reports that it can enable unauthenticated remote code execution in applications such as Jira, Jenkins and Keycloak2. Updated Java builds arrived on 17 November, with other distributions following on their own schedules1. The first question from the board was simple: where are we exposed? The SBOMs could not answer it, because they listed the libraries each application declared, not the Java runtime underneath.

What had to be true

  • Runtimes in the inventory, not only application libraries: Java, Python, Node and the operating system packages beneath them.
  • Vendor software included, with the components it bundles and the vendor's fix status.
  • Answers by query: which systems run an affected version, who owns them, and are they internet-facing.
  • One patch path: rebuild and redeploy, so what runs matches what was scanned.
  • Regulatory evidence as a by-product, not a separate spreadsheet.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: making the running estate match the inventory

An inventory is only as good as its link to what is actually running. Two things broke that link. First, Java arrived through many doors: base images from different teams, host packages, and vendor installers each bringing their own runtime. The fix was a small set of golden base images owned by the platform team, so patching Java meant changing one place and rebuilding everything that depended on it. Vendor products were tracked separately, with their bundled runtimes and the vendor's promised fix date recorded against them.

Second, people patched running systems by hand under pressure, which left containers that no longer matched their images. Kubernetes admission control can catch this: the Kubernetes blog describes a validating webhook that tags pods someone has run interactive commands in, and evicts them after a set interval so they are replaced from their declared state5. The team used the same idea, alongside a policy that only admits images built from current golden bases.

An SBOM tells you what you built. A runtime inventory tells you what you are running. For vulnerability response, only the second one matters.

Virtual machines and vendor-managed servers could not use admission control, so host discovery ran on a schedule and any runtime it found that was not in the inventory became a ticket with an owner. The approach builds on the legacy estate modernisation and vulnerability handling case studies, and on supply chain security patterns.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Scan images and hosts as well as buildsRely on build-time SBOMsRuntimes rarely appear in application manifests
A few golden base imagesEach team picks its own baseOne place to patch the runtime for everyone
Rebuild and redeployPatch running containersWhat runs stays identical to what was scanned
Vendor runtimes tracked with fix datesTreat vendor products as black boxesBundled Java is often the slowest part to fix
Time-limited exceptions with ownersOpen-ended risk acceptanceExceptions get reviewed instead of forgotten

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: treat the inventory as a product with an owner, and make regulatory SBOMs an export from it rather than a parallel effort. Differently: ask vendors for their bundled components and patch commitments at contract renewal, not during an incident. That was the slowest part of the response, and the only part the firm could not engineer its way out of. See vendor admin access as perimeter and the tech news for 19 November.

item.title: Tech news, 19 November 2026: Java4Shell, a poisoned Microsoft agent package, GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, and Malaysia's data centre pipeline
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: Java4Shell exposes Java servers to remote code execution, Microsoft's agent-framework package is poisoned on PyPI, and OpenAI ships GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol.
item.content:encoded:
A flaw in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder, dubbed Java4Shell, puts widely used Java servers at risk of remote code execution, and fixes are arriving unevenly across Java distributions. Two malicious releases of Microsoft's agent-framework package on PyPI stole cloud and CI credentials at Python start-up. OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, and Malaysia's parliament heard how large its approved data centre pipeline has become.

Today's brief covers stories from 17 to 18 November.

1. Java4Shell puts Java servers at risk of remote code execution

Researchers at Calif disclosed CVE-2026-114938, dubbed Java4Shell, a flaw in the Base64 decoder of OpenJDK's HotSpot runtime that can write outside its memory when handling malformed input; The Hacker News reports it can enable unauthenticated remote code execution in applications such as Jira, Jenkins and Keycloak1. Updated Java 17, 21, 25 and 27 builds were released on 17 November, and Qualys has published guidance on finding affected runtimes and patching2. Fixes are arriving at different times across Java distributions, and researchers note that turning it into working code execution takes work for each target1.

CTO take: the hard part is not the patch, it is finding every Java runtime: bundled inside vendor appliances, baked into container base images, pinned in old build pipelines. Start with internet-facing Java services and identity systems such as Keycloak, then rebuild images rather than patching running containers. Ask each vendor whose product ships its own Java when their fixed build lands, and track distributions separately, because Oracle's date is not your distribution's date. A software bill of materials that records the runtime, not just libraries, makes the next one of these a query instead of a hunt.

2. Microsoft's agent-framework package is poisoned on PyPI

Versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 of Microsoft's agent-framework package were published to PyPI on 17 November with a credential stealer that targeted Azure, Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions secrets3. The code ran through a .pth start-up hook, so it executed whenever Python started on an affected machine, even if the package was never imported; Wiz says 1.26.0 is the latest safe version4. Both releases have been removed.

CTO take: treat any machine or CI runner that installed either version as compromised and rotate every secret it could reach, not only the ones the reports name. The structural fix is the same as for every recent package attack: pin versions with hashes, let new releases age before automatic upgrades pick them up, and give CI jobs short-lived, narrowly scoped cloud credentials rather than long-lived secrets in environment variables. Agent frameworks are now core dependencies with broad access, so they deserve the controls you apply to payment code. See AI model supply chain security and vendor admin access as perimeter.

3. OpenAI releases GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol

OpenAI announced GPT-6.2 Astra, aimed at demanding professional work, and GPT-6.2 Sol, aimed at everyday and routine multi-step tasks, available in ChatGPT and Codex for paid plans and through the API5. Coverage reports lower API pricing for Astra and tighter safeguards on higher-risk cybersecurity requests6.

CTO take: a two-tier release is an invitation to route, not to switch. Run both against your own evaluation set, send routine work to the cheaper tier and keep the larger model for tasks where it measurably wins. If your product relies on security-related prompts, test whether the new safeguards change behaviour before upgrading. See LLM model routing and evaluation sets that predict production.

4. Malaysia's parliament hears the scale of its data centre pipeline

Malaysia's Dewan Rakyat was told on 18 November that the country's Data Centre Task Force had approved 27 projects worth an estimated RM225.97 billion up to last month, with lawmakers pressing for those investments to bring high-skilled jobs and strengthen AI and cybersecurity capability7.

CTO take: for companies across Southeast Asia, more local capacity means more choice of region and potentially lower latency, but also more scrutiny of what those facilities deliver locally and who uses their chips. If you plan to host AI workloads in Malaysia, check power and water commitments, export control obligations and local skills expectations alongside price. See the Malaysia GPU cloud case study and my work in Singapore and Southeast Asia.

What I'd do this week

  • Inventory Java runtimes, including those inside vendor products and container images; patch internet-facing services first.
  • Search lockfiles and CI logs for agent-framework 1.26.1 or 1.26.2; rotate secrets wherever it appears.
  • Add hash pinning and a release cooling-off period to Python and JavaScript dependency updates.
  • Evaluate GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol on your own tasks before changing defaults.
  • If Southeast Asian hosting is on your roadmap, add local policy and export control checks to provider selection.

item.title: Your vendors' admin tools are your perimeter: what N-central, ScreenConnect, Qubole and Optimizely have in common
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Four incidents in a month came through tools vendors use to manage customers. A CTO's take on standing vendor access, how to inventory it and how to shrink it.
item.content:encoded:
In the space of a few weeks, attackers went after a remote management platform, a remote support tool, a data platform's cross-account roles and an experimentation tag. Different products, one pattern: each is a channel a vendor uses to act inside many customers at once. Most companies have more of these channels than they know, and none of them shows up on a firewall diagram.

Four incidents, one pattern

N-able took its hosted N-central remote monitoring and management environments offline on 9 November after proof-of-concept exploits for more than 30 alleged flaws were published, and told on-premises customers to take their servers down1. A week later, attackers were exploiting a new N-central chain within hours of its proof of concept appearing2.

Meanwhile Huntress reported a campaign against managed service providers' ScreenConnect servers: between 20 October and 16 November, attackers posing as guests made around 688,000 requests across 42 servers to push a malicious file, waiting for a technician to join a session so a flaw in the technician's client would run it3. Wiz reported that an attacker used credentials tied to Qubole's AWS account to assume roles customers had created to trust Qubole, then collected secrets and data4. And attackers used a flaw in Optimizely's sign-up flow to inject malicious JavaScript into customer projects, which then ran on customers' websites5.

These are reported as four separate stories. They are one story. Each product is a channel a vendor uses to act inside many customers at once, and each attack went after the vendor's side of that channel rather than the customer's front door.

Where vendor access actually lives

Most organisations can list their suppliers. Far fewer can list what each supplier can do inside their environment right now, without asking. That second list is the one that matters.

The common property is that the access is standing: it exists whether or not the vendor is doing anything for you today, and it is protected by the vendor's security, not yours. A remote management agent that can run any command at any time is the same risk on a quiet Sunday as it is during a support call.

Put vendor actions through the same gates as your own

The useful model comes from platforms that already treat every caller the same way. In Kubernetes, every request to the API server, from a person or from a workload, passes authentication, then authorisation, then admission control before it changes anything7. Vendor access usually skips most of that: the agent is authenticated once at install and then trusted for everything.

Applied to suppliers, that means three questions for every channel. Who is acting: the vendor's platform, or a named technician with strong sign-in? What may they do: everything, or a defined set of actions on a defined set of systems? And what checks the action at the moment it happens: nothing, or a policy, an approval or at least a record someone reviews?

Cloud providers have built some of this already. AWS documents the confused deputy problem for exactly the Qubole pattern, and recommends conditions such as an external ID on roles that third parties assume6. That helps against one customer tricking a vendor into acting on another's account. It does not help when the vendor's own credentials are stolen, which is why narrowing what each role can reach matters as much as how it is assumed.

What to do: a short programme, not a project

ChannelThis month's exampleFirst thing to change
Remote managementN-central exploits1Limit which machines the agent covers and what scripts it may run
Remote supportScreenConnect technician attacks3Patch technician clients; block file transfer by guests; record sessions
Cross-account cloud rolesQubole roles assumed4Remove unused roles; keep secrets out of what roles can read
Third-party scriptsOptimizely injection5Keep vendor scripts off payment and login pages; restrict with a Content Security Policy

The test is simple: if a vendor told you at 3am that its platform was compromised, could you cut its access to you within the hour, and know what it had done in the last month? If not, start there.

The conversation with your managed service provider

Many mid-sized companies reach remote management and remote support tools only through a managed service provider, so the exposure is real but the controls belong to someone else. That makes the contract and the questions the control. Ask which tools they run on your systems and at what versions, how technician accounts sign in, whether sessions are recorded and whether you can see the logs, and how they would tell you about a compromise of their own tooling. The MSP cyber resilience case study shows what a provider that takes this seriously looks like from the inside.

For cloud and SaaS access, the same thinking runs through the third-party cloud access case study and the machine identity case study. For web scripts, see the payment page script security case study, and for AI vendors specifically, AI inference providers are now supply chain.

The CTO's take

Supplier risk is usually run as paperwork: questionnaires, certificates, annual reviews. This month showed it is an engineering problem. The question is not whether a vendor is reputable, but how much it can do inside your environment without you noticing, and how fast you can stop it. Those are things you can measure, reduce and rehearse.

item.title: Reasonable steps you can prove: preparing an Australian bank for the Scams Prevention Framework
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How an Australian bank can prepare for the Scams Prevention Framework: scam intelligence, real-time payment friction, fast disruption and evidence of reasonable steps.
item.content:encoded:
A customer-owned Australian bank had fraud controls built for stolen cards and taken-over accounts, not for customers persuaded to send money themselves. The Scams Prevention Framework turns scam prevention into a legal duty with a regulator watching. The goal was a platform that finds scams earlier, acts on intelligence quickly and can show, payment by payment, why it did what it did.

The situation

A mid-sized, customer-owned Australian bank had sound fraud controls for the problems of a decade ago: stolen card numbers, compromised passwords, account takeover. Its losses had shifted to a different pattern. Customers were being talked into sending money themselves, through investment, impersonation and romance scams, and the bank's systems saw a properly authenticated customer making a real-time payment. Every control said the payment was legitimate, because technically it was.

The Scams Prevention Framework changes what a bank is expected to do about that. Passed in February 2025, it sets overarching principles for designated sectors: governance, prevent, detect, report, disrupt and respond1. When a bank has actionable scam intelligence, meaning reasonable grounds to suspect a scam connected with its service, it must report it to the ACCC and take reasonable steps to disrupt it, with a safe harbour for disruption while it investigates, for up to 28 days2.

Why now. Banking, telecommunications and digital platforms have been designated as the first sectors, and the framework is moving from principles to detailed sector codes4. Treasury released draft rules and codes, including a common code and a banking code, for consultation in May 20263. The obligations are close enough that the platform work had to start now, not after the final text.

What had to be true

  • Scams treated as their own problem, not as a subset of unauthorised fraud.
  • One view of a scam across payments, devices, customer reports and intelligence from other organisations.
  • Friction that matches risk: most payments untouched, the risky few slowed in ways that actually break the scammer's script.
  • Intelligence acted on in hours, with reporting and disruption tracked as work, not emails.
  • Evidence for every intervention, strong enough for a complaint, an external dispute or the regulator.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: proving reasonable steps, case by case

A framework built on reasonable steps is judged after the event. A customer complains weeks later; the question is what the bank knew at the moment of the payment, and what it did. Fraud systems usually keep a score and an outcome. That is not enough. The design stored an immutable decision record for every payment that was scored above the lowest threshold: the signals present, the rule or model version, the friction shown and the customer's response.

Traces were the second layer. Keeping a full trace for every payment would be expensive and mostly useless. Tail sampling in the OpenTelemetry Collector makes the keep-or-drop decision after all spans in a trace are complete5, so the team kept every trace for a flagged, held or interrupted payment and a small sample of the rest.

Traces cannot be the only record. A scam reported a week later was never flagged at the time, so its trace may be gone. The decision record is the evidence; traces are the detail when you still have them.

The entity graph followed the approach in the fraud ring knowledge graph, using entity resolution to connect payees, mule accounts, phone numbers and websites across reports. The LLM triage step turned free-text customer reports into structured intelligence, with a person confirming anything that would trigger disruption; it was evaluated on real, de-identified reports first, as in evaluation sets that predict production.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Separate scam models from fraud modelsExtend the existing fraud modelThe customer is genuine; the signals and the right response are different
Targeted friction, such as a scam-specific questionGeneric warnings on every paymentCustomers learn to click past generic warnings
Intelligence as cases with owners and clocksAlerts in a shared inboxReporting and disruption must be timely and provable
Person confirms LLM-extracted intelligenceAutomatic action on model outputWrongly blocking a payee harms a real customer
Decision records for every scored paymentRely on logs and tracesLogs rotate; complaints arrive weeks later
Build to the principles, track the codesWait for final codesThe principles are stable; the detail can be tuned

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: start with the evidence record and the case model, because they shape everything else, and treat the regulator's definition of actionable intelligence as an engineering requirement with a threshold and an owner. Differently: bring operations and the contact centre in on friction design from the first week. The best interventions came from the people who talk to scam victims, not from the risk model. Related patterns are in idempotent payment pipelines and deepfake-resistant onboarding.
