item.title: Tech news, 18 November 2026: the Optimizely supply chain attack, Nvidia's first results without Huang, New York's AI enforcement unit and Microsoft's MAI Code 2
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: attackers inject malware via Optimizely into 178 sites, Nvidia beats and raises in its first post-Huang results, New York forms an AI enforcement unit.
item.content:encoded:
Attackers used a flaw in Optimizely's experimentation platform to inject malicious JavaScript into the websites of 178 organisations, a reminder that every third-party script runs with your site's full trust. Nvidia reported strong results and raised guidance in its first quarter under an interim chief executive, New York set up a unit to enforce its AI safety law, and Microsoft released cheaper coding models.

Today's brief covers stories from 16 to 17 November.

1. Attackers inject malware into 178 websites through Optimizely

Optimizely said an unauthorised party exploited a flaw in its Experimentation account sign-up flow to inject malicious JavaScript into some customer projects; Report URI identified infected snippets across 178 organisations, including major media and technology brands1. The Register reports the code targeted visitors' payment details and cryptocurrency transfers, and Optimizely says it fixed the flaw, removed the code, revoked tokens and notified customers2.

CTO take: any third-party script on your site runs with your site's full trust. List every script you load, keep testing, analytics and marketing tags off payment and login pages, restrict what scripts can do with a Content Security Policy, monitor scripts for unexpected changes and make sure you can switch a vendor's tag off in minutes. Payment card rules already require monitoring of scripts on payment pages; this shows why. See the payment page script security case study.

2. Nvidia beats and raises in its first results without Huang

Nvidia reported third-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $115.8 billion, with data centre revenue of $107.6 billion, and guided next-quarter revenue to about $130 billion3. CNBC notes it was the company's first report since Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive, with Colette Kress serving as interim CEO4.

CTO take: demand for AI hardware is still rising, which means capacity stays tight and expensive for most buyers into next year. Plan for that: commit to capacity only where usage is proven, make models cheaper to run, and keep your stack portable across providers. See AI capacity contracts.

3. New York creates a unit to enforce its AI safety law

New York Attorney General Letitia James announced an AI Safety, Standards, Enforcement and Transparency unit, which her office describes as the first in the country dedicated to enforcing AI laws, and which will enforce the state's RAISE Act for frontier AI developers5.

CTO take: enforcement capacity is following the laws. The direct duties fall on large model developers, but expect providers to ask customers for help with incident reporting and to update terms. Keep a record of the AI models you use and how; see the board AI briefing checklist and the US page.

4. Microsoft releases MAI Code 2 for coding

Microsoft announced MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash at Ignite, available in GitHub Copilot, alongside other new MAI models; Microsoft's own benchmarks claim performance close to leading frontier models at a much lower price6.

CTO take: coding model choice is becoming a cost lever, not just a quality one. Test new models on your own repositories and tasks before switching, and keep your coding agent policy independent of any one model; see AI coding policy for engineering teams.

What I'd do this week

  • Inventory third-party scripts on your sites and remove any from payment and login pages.
  • Add or tighten a Content Security Policy and script change monitoring.
  • Revisit AI capacity plans in light of continued tight supply.
  • Trial new coding models on real tasks before changing defaults.

item.title: Paying down technical debt without a rewrite: what works when the business cannot stop
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a fractional CTO paydown plan works in practice: name the debt by its business cost, fund it like a portfolio and replace systems piece by piece instead of rewriting.
item.content:encoded:
Almost every company I join has a system everyone wants to rewrite. Almost none of those rewrites should happen. Debt is real and expensive, but the cure is usually a steady, funded paydown that the business can see, not a big-bang replacement that freezes product work for a year. This is how I approach it, and how I explain it to founders and boards.

The rewrite that never ships

The pattern is familiar. A core system has grown slow to change and fragile to run. Engineers propose a rewrite. Leadership agrees, because it sounds decisive. A year later the new system handles some of the work, the old one still handles the rest, and the team now maintains both. Product work slowed the whole time.

Ward Cunningham, who coined the term, described debt as the cost of shipping with understanding that later needs to be repaid by refactoring; the danger is not borrowing but never repaying1. Repayment works best in small, regular instalments, not one enormous one.

Step 1: name debt by what it costs the business

"The code is messy" is not a reason a board can fund. "Every change to pricing takes three teams and a weekend release" is. I start by listing debt items with their business effect: what they slow down, what they put at risk and what manual work they create. Martin Fowler's distinction between deliberate and inadvertent, prudent and reckless debt helps separate conscious trade-offs worth keeping from accidents worth fixing2.

Toil deserves special attention. Google's SRE guidance defines it as manual, repetitive work that scales with the service and has no lasting value5; it is often the cheapest debt to pay down and the easiest to show results for.

Step 2: fund it like a portfolio

Instead of a one-off project, agree an explicit share of engineering capacity for debt and reliability work, and protect it. The exact share depends on the state of the system and the business's appetite; what matters is that it is visible, agreed and not raided every time a deadline looms.

Then measure whether it is working. The four DORA measures, deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore, are a good, widely understood signal of whether paydown is making delivery faster and safer4. If they do not move, change what you are paying down.

Debt paydown that cannot show its effect on delivery or risk will lose its budget. Measure it, report it and connect it to things the business already cares about.

Step 3: replace piece by piece

When part of a system really does need replacing, the strangler fig approach works far better than a rewrite: put a stable interface in front of the old system, build new capability behind it one slice at a time, and gradually route traffic to the new parts until the old system can be retired3.

Modern routing makes the shift step routine. Weighted routing can send a small share of traffic to the new implementation, or route specific requests by header, and roll back instantly if something goes wrong6.

When a rewrite is actually right

SituationUsually better
System works but is slow to changeRefactor and replace slices
Platform is unsupported or insecure with no upgrade pathPlanned migration, still in slices where possible
Small system with clear, stable requirementsA rewrite can be reasonable
Business model has changed completelyBuild new alongside, retire old

Even when replacement is justified, I push to run old and new in parallel and move traffic gradually. The goal is never a "big bang" day.

Field note: what I tell founders

Three things. First, debt is a normal cost of moving fast; the question is whether you are paying the interest knowingly. Second, the team that wants a rewrite is usually right about the pain and wrong about the cure. Third, the best signal of progress is not new architecture diagrams but faster, safer releases and fewer late-night incidents. item.title: Know your compute customer: building export-control compliance into a Malaysian GPU cloud
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a Malaysian GPU cloud provider can build export-control compliance into its platform: customer screening, policy-gated GPU access and evidence of where compute goes.
item.content:encoded:
A Malaysian data centre operator had added a GPU cloud to serve regional AI start-ups, enterprises and research labs. Demand was strong. So was scrutiny: Malaysia had introduced permits for moving US-origin AI chips, and in November 2026 the US moved to require licences for advanced chips going to Malaysia and four other countries, including to stop restricted parties reaching them remotely. The operator needed to prove, continuously, who was using its GPUs and for what, without becoming impossible to buy from.

The situation

A Malaysian data centre operator added a GPU cloud to its colocation business, offering training and inference capacity to start-ups, enterprises and university labs across South-East Asia. Customers signed up online, were given a Kubernetes namespace and GPU quota, and could start work within a day. Onboarding checked payment details and little else.

Malaysia had already tightened its own controls: since July 2025, exporting, transshipping or moving US-origin high-performance AI chips through the country requires a permit under the Strategic Trade Act34. The operator's hardware stayed in its own halls, so that rule mostly affected its suppliers. The bigger question was who was using the hardware remotely.

Why now. In November 2026, the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security issued a rule requiring licences for advanced AI chips going to Malaysia, Indonesia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, and aimed at stopping restricted parties from reaching controlled chips through data centres in third countries12. For a GPU cloud in Malaysia, that made its customer list part of its supply chain: future hardware purchases would depend on being able to show where compute went.

What had to be true

  • Known customers: every tenant screened, including who ultimately owns or controls it.
  • Gated access: no GPU capacity until checks are complete, and access paused if they lapse.
  • Known users: every person and service using a tenant's GPUs identifiable.
  • Traceable usage: who used which GPUs, when and from where, kept as evidence.
  • Watchful: unusual patterns surfaced for review.
  • Still easy to buy: legitimate customers onboard in days, not months.

Architecture

The platform already used Kueue to queue and admit GPU jobs fairly across tenants. That admission step became the enforcement point. Each tenant's queue was linked to its compliance status: if screening was incomplete, had expired or was under review, the tenant's jobs stayed suspended rather than running. Kueue's model of jobs waiting in a queue until admitted made this a configuration change rather than a new system5.

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: remote access and changing customers

Who is really using the GPUs? A screened customer can resell capacity, share credentials or be acquired. The operator required named user identities with multi-factor sign-in, prohibited credential sharing and resale without approval in its terms, and logged where each session came from. Monitoring looked for patterns worth a human look: many users appearing under one small tenant, access from unexpected locations, or workloads that did not match the declared use.

Rescreening without friction. Ownership and restricted-party lists change. Rather than rescreen everyone at once, the platform rescreened tenants on a schedule and whenever lists were updated or a tenant's details changed, pausing only those with new matches for review. Legitimate customers rarely noticed.

Not a law firm. Export-control questions often need legal judgement. The platform's job was to collect facts and enforce decisions consistently; edge cases went to compliance staff and external counsel, and their decisions were recorded alongside the evidence.

For a GPU cloud, the customer list is now part of the hardware supply chain. Build compliance into the scheduler, not a spreadsheet, so it cannot be bypassed on a busy day.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Enforce in the schedulerManual checks before provisioningCannot be skipped under pressure
Suspend jobs, do not delete tenantsTerminate access on any doubtReview without losing customers' work
Named users with MFAShared tenant credentialsKnow who actually uses the GPUs
Event-driven rescreeningAnnual review onlyCatches changes when they happen
Humans decide edge casesFully automated decisionsLegal judgement stays with people
Evidence store from day oneAssemble evidence when askedSupports licences and audits quickly

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: put enforcement in the admission step of the scheduler; it made compliance consistent without slowing engineers. Differently: involve the hardware suppliers earlier, since their own export obligations shaped what evidence they needed from the operator. item.title: Tech news, 17 November 2026: US licences for AI chips to five countries, a Nordic AI gigafactory consortium, AMD closes World Labs and a nervous week for AI stocks
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: the US requires licences for AI chips to five countries, a Nordic AI gigafactory bid forms, AMD closes World Labs and AI stocks slide.
item.content:encoded:
The US moved to require licences for advanced AI chips going to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, including to curb remote access through overseas data centres. In Europe, five companies formed a consortium to bid for an EU AI gigafactory. AMD completed its purchase of World Labs, and AI stocks fell ahead of Nvidia's results and Anthropic's expected listing.

Today's brief covers stories from 15 to 16 November.

1. The US requires licences for advanced AI chips to five countries

The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security issued a rule requiring licences for exports of advanced AI chips and the systems containing them to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, citing diversion risk, DCD reports1. Nextgov reports the rule also aims to stop controls being circumvented through remote access to data centres in third countries; reporting says companies headquartered in the US are exempt if they meet reporting requirements2.

CTO take: if you use or plan GPU capacity in South-East Asia or Brazil through non-US providers, expect new paperwork, delays and possibly higher prices. Ask providers how the rule affects their supply and existing contracts, and keep alternatives in other regions. If you operate data centres in these markets, know your customers and where their ownership sits. See AI capacity contracts and the Singapore page.

2. Five European firms form a consortium to bid for an EU AI gigafactory

Nokia, Nscale, Skeleton, Telia and Verda formed AI Gigafactory Northern to bid in the EU's AI gigafactory programme, proposing one AI facility spread across sites in the Nordic and Baltic region3. The Next Web reports initial sites in Finland, Estonia and Latvia, with a Swedish site to be confirmed4.

CTO take: European sovereign AI capacity is moving from policy to bids, but it will take years to arrive. If EU data residency or sovereignty matters to your customers, plan with today's providers and watch these projects as future options rather than near-term capacity. See the sovereign LLM platform case study and the Europe page.

3. AMD completes its acquisition of World Labs

AMD said it completed its acquisition of World Labs, which builds models that create and simulate interactive 3D environments, and that co-founder Fei-Fei Li joins AMD as executive vice president and chief scientist5.

CTO take: chipmakers are buying model and research teams to make their hardware more attractive. For buyers, more credible alternatives to a single accelerator vendor are good news, but only if your software stack can use them. Keep serving layers portable across hardware where you can.

4. AI stocks slide ahead of a big week

US tech stocks fell on 16 November, with AI-linked names hit hardest, ahead of Nvidia's quarterly results and Anthropic's expected market debut later in the week, CNN reports6.

CTO take: market swings rarely change engineering plans, but they shape the financing behind AI capacity and pricing. Keep contracts flexible and avoid building on a single provider whose economics you cannot see.

What I'd do this week

  • Ask GPU and AI cloud providers in South-East Asia and Brazil how the new US rule affects them.
  • Check where your AI capacity is planned and whether it relies on a single region or provider.
  • Review how portable your model serving is across hardware vendors.

item.title: Meta's €805 million fine: what on-device data, consent and AI features mean for product teams in Europe
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Italy fined Meta €805M for reading phone galleries without specific consent. A CTO's take on device access rules in the EU and how to design AI features around them.
item.content:encoded:
Italy's data protection authority fined Meta €805 million because a Facebook feature, on by default, read photos, videos and metadata from Android phones without specific consent. The striking part is not the size of the fine but the principle: in the EU, reading data on a user's device needs consent even if nothing leaves the phone. As AI features look for more on-device context, that principle reaches far beyond Meta.

What the Garante decided

Italy's data protection authority fined Meta €805 million over the Facebook Android app's gallery suggestions feature, which was on by default and proposed photos and videos from users' phones to post; the authority found it accessed photos, videos and metadata without specific, informed consent1. Meta must ask for consent through a separate, specific prompt, keep the feature off by default and report back to the regulator; Meta said it strongly disagrees and will appeal23.

The legal basis matters more than the number. The decision rests on the rule, from the EU ePrivacy Directive, that storing or accessing information on a user's device requires consent unless it is strictly necessary for a service the user asked for4. Reporting notes the authority treated that requirement as applying whether or not data left the phone1.

Why this matters beyond Meta

Many product teams assume that processing data locally is automatically privacy-friendly and needs no special permission. The European Data Protection Board's guidelines on the technical scope of the device access rule take a broader view: the rule turns on gaining access to information on the device, and the guidelines discuss local processing among their use cases5. On-device processing is often good privacy engineering; it is not, by itself, a consent exemption.

AI features make this sharper. Assistants that read photos to suggest posts, scan messages to draft replies, index files to answer questions or use sensors for context all reach into the device. The more context a feature uses, the more it looks like the gallery suggestions feature the Garante fined.

Designing AI features that use device data

Off by default. If a feature reads personal content from the device and is not strictly necessary for something the user explicitly asked for, ship it off and let users turn it on.

A specific, honest prompt. Ask at the moment the feature is first useful, in plain words: what will be read, why, whether anything leaves the device, and how to turn it off. The operating system's permission dialog is not enough on its own; it says what the app can access, not what your feature does with it. The same pattern works inside AI assistants: an in-context confirmation that says exactly what will happen before it does6.

Minimum access. Ask for the narrowest access that works: selected photos rather than the whole gallery, one folder rather than all files, approximate rather than precise location.

Records. Keep a record of what each user agreed to, when and in which version of the prompt, so you can show it later and re-ask when the feature changes.

Same rules for models. If device content is sent to a server or a third-party model, say so, minimise it and apply your normal data protection controls. If it is used to train models, that is a separate purpose needing its own basis.

On-device processing is good engineering, not a legal shortcut. In the EU, if your feature reaches into the phone, ask first, ask specifically and start switched off.

A quick review for existing features

CTO take

This fine is about consent and defaults, not about whether the feature was useful. As products add AI that looks for more context, the easiest way to stay on the right side of EU rules is to treat device content as something users lend you deliberately, not something you collect because the permission dialog allowed it. Product, engineering and legal should review device-reading features together, and new AI features should come with a consent design from day one. Meta has said it will appeal, so the decision may change; the design principles will not. Read alongside the 16 November tech news, the data protection programme case study and the Europe page.

item.title: Change without fear: progressive rollouts and fast rollback for a Brazilian payments platform
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a Brazilian payments platform can change safely at 1M+ transactions a day: progressive rollouts, canaries judged on payment signals and fast rollback.
item.content:encoded:
A Brazilian payment institution processed more than a million transactions a day, most of them instant payments that customers expect to complete in seconds. Most of its incidents were not caused by attackers or hardware, but by its own changes: a configuration tweak, a library upgrade, a network adjustment. After a major provider's long outage was traced to a routine network change exposing a latent bug, the company decided to make every change small, observable and reversible.

The situation

A Brazilian payment institution offered accounts, cards and instant payments to consumers and small businesses, processing more than a million transactions a day. Customers expected instant payments to complete in seconds at any hour, and partners expected the same. The platform ran on Kubernetes across two cloud regions, with dozens of services owned by several teams.

Its post-incident reviews told a consistent story. The serious incidents rarely came from attacks or hardware. They came from the company's own changes: a configuration value changed everywhere at once, a library upgrade that behaved differently under peak load, a network rule adjusted during maintenance. Code deployments had some safeguards; configuration and network changes had almost none.

Brazil's National Monetary Council requires regulated institutions to maintain a cybersecurity policy with incident response and to manage risks in data processing and cloud services5. The company's resilience depended as much on how it changed its own systems as on any external threat.

Why now. In November 2026, Microsoft attributed a long Microsoft 365 outage to traffic shifts during routine network maintenance exposing a latent bug from an earlier capacity upgrade12. If one of the world's largest operators could be caught by a routine network change, the board asked, what protected a payments platform from the same pattern?

What had to be true

  • Every change counted: code, configuration, infrastructure and network changes all go through a controlled path.
  • Small first: changes reach a small slice of traffic before everyone.
  • Judged by customers: health measured by payment success and latency, not server metrics alone.
  • Reversible: rollback is fast, rehearsed and the default when in doubt.
  • Visible: anyone can see what changed, where and when, during an incident.
  • Still fast: teams ship often; safety comes from smaller changes, not fewer.

Architecture

Code deployments moved to progressive rollouts on Kubernetes: a new version first replaced a small number of pods while the rest kept serving, and only continued if it stayed healthy. Google's SRE guidance describes canarying in exactly these terms: test each change on a small slice of traffic so defects are caught early with limited impact3.

The bigger change was bringing configuration and network changes into the same discipline6. Configuration moved into version control and rolled out by region and by service in stages, with the same health checks as code. Network changes, such as firewall rules, load balancer settings and routing, went through a pipeline that applied them to one zone first and watched payment signals before continuing.

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: judging health in a payments system

Choosing signals that reflect customers. Server metrics often looked fine while customers suffered. Canary analysis used signals that matched customer experience: payment success rate by payment type and partner, end-to-end latency, error codes returned to apps and depth of downstream queues. The SRE workbook stresses choosing metrics that genuinely indicate problems and comparing the canary against a control rather than a fixed threshold3.

Low-volume paths and latent bugs. A canary on a small slice of traffic can miss problems in rare paths, such as an unusual partner or a refund flow, and latent bugs may only appear under peak load. The team added synthetic transactions for rare paths, kept each wave long enough to cover a busy period for critical changes, and avoided large changes during known peaks such as month-end and holidays.

Rollback as the default. Engineers used to try to fix forward during incidents. The new rule: if a recent change might be involved, roll it back first and investigate afterwards. Rollback was rehearsed regularly, and the change timeline appeared on every dashboard so responders could see what had just changed. Google's release engineering guidance treats reliable, repeatable releases and rollbacks as foundations of reliability4.

Most outages are self-inflicted. Make every change small, watched and reversible, including the configuration and network changes nobody thinks of as releases.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Stage configuration and network changesStage code onlyMany serious incidents start outside code
Judge canaries on payment signalsCPU and memory thresholdsCustomers feel payments, not servers
Compare canary with controlFixed thresholdsHandles daily traffic patterns
Rollback first, investigate laterFix forwardShorter incidents, calmer responders
Synthetic checks for rare pathsRely on live canary trafficLow-volume flows still get tested
Peak calendar for large changesShip anytimeReduces risk when impact would be highest

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: put every change, of every type, on one timeline overlaid on dashboards; it shortened incidents before any automation existed. Differently: bring network engineering in from the start rather than after the code pipeline was done; network changes turned out to carry the most risk and the least tooling. item.title: Tech news, 16 November 2026: Italy fines Meta €805 million, Microsoft explains its outage, Maileva's 22 million-person leak and a new N-able exploit
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: Italy fines Meta €805M over Android gallery access, Microsoft explains its outage, a La Poste unit leaks 22M records and N-able is hit again.
item.content:encoded:
Italy's data protection authority fined Meta €805 million for accessing phone galleries without proper consent, a reminder that device permissions are personal data decisions. Microsoft gave a preliminary cause for last week's outage, a French mail platform confirmed a leak affecting 22 million people, and attackers exploited a new chain against N-able's remote management servers.

Today's brief covers stories from 13 to 15 November.

1. Italy fines Meta €805 million over Android gallery access

Italy's data protection authority, the Garante, fined Meta €805 million because the Facebook Android app's gallery suggestions feature, on by default, accessed photos, videos and metadata on users' phones without specific, informed consent, Security Affairs reports1. Meta must ask for separate consent and keep the feature off by default; it said it strongly disagrees and will appeal2.

CTO take: in the EU, reading data from a user's device needs consent even if nothing leaves the phone. Any app feature that touches photos, contacts, files or sensors should be off by default, explained in a specific prompt and logged. As AI features look for more context from devices, this ruling sets the bar; product and legal should review them together. See the Europe page.

2. Microsoft gives a preliminary cause for its outage

Microsoft said traffic shifts during routine network maintenance exposed a latent bug from an earlier capacity upgrade, causing connection requests to queue until servers ran out of processing capacity; it found no sign of malicious activity3. ARN reports the disruption lasted about 30 hours and that Microsoft will publish a full post-incident review4.

CTO take: latent bugs exposed by later changes are among the hardest failures to prevent, even for the largest operators. The lesson for your own systems is to test changes against realistic load and to make rollback fast; the lesson for your suppliers is to plan as if this will happen again. See the Microsoft 365 outage playbook.

3. A La Poste subsidiary confirms a leak affecting 22 million people

Maileva, an online mail service in La Poste's Docaposte group, confirmed on 14 November that names and postal addresses of around 22 million people were stolen in a September attack, Ouest-France reports5. The people affected were recipients of mail sent by Maileva's business customers.

CTO take: if you send letters, invoices or notices through a print-and-post provider, your customers' data sits with that provider. Include such services in your supplier inventory, ask how long they keep recipient data and whether they need to keep it at all, and prepare to answer your own customers' questions.

4. A new N-able N-central exploit chain is in use

Attackers began exploiting a new chain against N-able N-central remote management servers, dubbed 4EverAble2Shell, within hours of a proof of concept being released, BleepingComputer reports6.

CTO take: this is the second wave against N-central in a week. If your managed service provider runs it, ask for confirmation that their servers are patched or offline, and consider restricting what their remote management agents can do on your systems until they are. See the third-party access case study.

What I'd do this week

  • Review app features that read device data and make sure consent is specific and defaults are off.
  • Read Microsoft's post-incident review when published and update your outage plan.
  • Add print, mail and notification providers to your supplier inventory.
  • Get written confirmation from your managed service provider about N-central.

item.title: What your board needs to know about your AI: a CTO's checklist for a briefing that leads to decisions
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A practical checklist for briefing a board on AI: where it is used, what it costs, how it could fail, which rules apply and what decisions the board must own.
item.content:encoded:
Most boards now ask about AI, and most AI briefings either drown directors in model names or reassure them with demos. Neither helps them govern. A good briefing tells the board where AI is used, what it costs, how it could fail, which rules apply and which decisions are theirs. This is the checklist I use, built on the frameworks regulators and auditors increasingly expect, and it fits on a few pages.

Why most AI briefings fail

Boards do not need to understand transformers. They need to know whether AI is creating value, what could go wrong, whether management has it under control and what they must decide. Briefings fail when they answer a different question: technical detail directors cannot judge, or optimistic demos that hide risk. The fix is a consistent structure, repeated every time, so directors can see change over time.

Established frameworks help. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework organises the work into governing, mapping, measuring and managing AI risk1, and ISO/IEC 42001 sets out requirements for an AI management system2. You do not need certification to borrow their structure; it gives directors and auditors a vocabulary they will increasingly recognise.

The checklist

1. An inventory of AI in use. One page listing each significant use: what it does, who uses it, whether customers see it, what data it touches and who owns it. Include AI inside bought software, not only what you build. If you cannot produce this page, that is the first finding.

2. Value and cost. For each major use, what it costs (models, infrastructure, people) and what it returns, in the board's terms: revenue, cost avoided, time saved, risk reduced. Show trends, not just a snapshot. Telemetry recording model, tokens and outcome per call makes this possible6.

3. The top risks and how they are controlled. Five or six risks at most, each with its controls and how you know they work: wrong or harmful outputs, data exposure, agents acting beyond their scope, supplier failure, bias in decisions about people, and cost overruns. Say plainly which are under control and which are not.

4. Supplier dependence. Which model and infrastructure providers you rely on, what you send them, and how quickly you could move. Recent breaches at AI providers, and outages at major platforms, make this a board-level question; see AI inference providers are supply chain.

5. Rules by market. Which laws apply where you operate: the EU AI Act's obligations, including AI literacy for staff4; new national regimes such as Australia's planned rules for frontier developers5; data protection and sector rules. Show what is in force, what is coming and what you are doing about each.

6. Incidents and near misses. What went wrong since the last briefing, including near misses, and what changed as a result. A briefing with no incidents usually means incidents are not being recorded.

7. Principles and red lines. What the company will not do with AI, aligned with widely accepted principles such as the OECD's on transparency, robustness and accountability3. Directors should approve these, not just note them.

8. Decisions for the board. End with specific asks: approve a risk appetite statement, fund a capability, accept or reject a risk, agree a red line. A briefing without a decision is an update, and boards stop reading updates.

A one-page format

SectionWhat goes in itSignal to watch
InventoryUses, owners, data, customer-facing or notNew uses appearing without review
Value and costCost and return per major useCost rising faster than value
RisksTop risks, controls, statusRisks stuck at "not controlled"
SuppliersKey providers, data shared, exit timeSingle points of failure
RulesLaws by market, deadlines, actionsDeadlines without owners
IncidentsWhat happened, what changedNo incidents reported at all
DecisionsSpecific asks of the boardDecisions deferred repeatedly

Boards govern what they can see. Give them the same few pages every time, with trends, red flags and a decision, and they will govern AI as well as they govern anything else.

How to build it the first time

Pre-brief the chair and any director with a technology or risk background before the meeting. It improves the questions you get and avoids surprises. Afterwards, record the decisions and fold them into the next briefing.

CTO take

AI governance is not a separate discipline from running a technology function well; it is the same discipline applied to a fast-moving area. The CTO's job is to make AI legible to the board: what it is, what it is worth, what could go wrong and what they need to decide. Doing that well also forces the inventory, cost tracking and risk controls that the organisation needs anyway. See a fractional CTO's first 90 days, AI literacy under the EU AI Act and the AI governance programme case study.

item.title: Testing with the regulator in the room: an EU medtech start-up's hospital early-warning model in an AI regulatory sandbox
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How an EU medtech start-up can use the new AI regulatory sandbox rules for a hospital early-warning model: a clear test plan, real-world evidence and no false comfort.
item.content:encoded:
A European medtech start-up had built a model that warns hospital ward staff when a patient is likely to deteriorate. It worked on historical data. The questions that mattered next were harder: would it hold up on live wards, how should nurses act on it, and what would regulators expect as evidence? When the EU set common rules for AI regulatory sandboxes, the start-up decided to answer those questions in one, with a supervisor watching, without mistaking the sandbox for approval.

The situation

A European medtech start-up had developed a model that estimates the risk that a patient on a general hospital ward will deteriorate in the next day, using vital signs, laboratory results and nursing observations. On historical data from two partner hospitals it performed well. The founders knew that was the easy part. Clinical AI often fails in the move from historical data to live wards: data arrives late or differently, staff respond to alerts in ways nobody predicted, and performance varies between sites and patient groups.

As software intended to support clinical decisions, the product was likely to be regulated as a medical device and treated as high-risk under the EU AI Act. The team needed evidence that would satisfy both regimes, and had no experience of what supervisors would expect.

Why now. On 11 November 2026, the Commission published Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2487, setting common rules for establishing and running AI regulatory sandboxes under the AI Act12. Commentary was quick to point out the limits: sandbox participation produces documentation and an exit report, not compliance clearance, and liability stays with the provider34. That suited the start-up: it wanted structured supervision and early feedback, not a shortcut.

What had to be true

  • Clear questions: the sandbox plan states exactly what will be tested and what success looks like.
  • Patient safety first: no clinician acts on the model until it has been validated on live data.
  • Evidence that travels: results usable later for the AI Act and medical device assessments.
  • Performance by group: results reported by site, ward type and patient group.
  • Reproducible: any result can be regenerated from versioned data, features and model.
  • No false comfort: everyone understands what the sandbox does and does not provide.

Architecture

Hospital data arrived through FHIR feeds into a feature pipeline where every feature had a versioned definition, so a result could always be traced to the exact data and code that produced it. The scoring service ran in two modes: silent, where scores were stored but not shown, and live, where alerts reached ward staff. See healthcare data architecture.

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: evidence a supervisor can trust

Designing the sandbox plan. The start-up's first draft asked to "test the model in hospitals". The final plan, agreed with the supervising authority, asked specific questions: does performance on live data match historical results at each site; is the model well calibrated for older patients and patients with chronic conditions; do nurses act on alerts within the expected time; and does alert volume stay manageable on busy wards. Each question had a success criterion and an agreed response if it failed.

Making results reproducible and generalisable. Supervisors and later assessors would ask whether results could be repeated and whether they would hold elsewhere. The team borrowed the vocabulary of the observational research community: a result should be repeatable on the same data, reproducible by someone else, and generalisable to different data5. Versioned data and features handled the first two; adding a third hospital partway through tested the last.

Silent mode before live mode. For the first phase the model scored real patients but showed nothing to clinicians. That exposed data timing problems at one site that would have made live alerts arrive too late to help, and a calibration gap in one patient group that was fixed before any nurse saw a score.

A sandbox is valuable for what you learn with the supervisor watching, not for the badge. Go in with sharp questions, and come out with evidence you would have needed anyway.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Enter a sandbox with specific questionsTreat it as a general pilotClear questions make supervisor feedback useful
Silent mode before live alertsGo live on validated historyLive data behaves differently; patients stay safe
Report by site and patient groupOne overall scoreAverages hide where the model fails
Versioned features and dataAd hoc extractsResults can be reproduced for assessors
Add a third hospital mid-sandboxStay with two partnersTests whether results generalise
Plan conformity assessment in parallelRely on the exit reportThe sandbox does not grant compliance

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: write the sandbox questions with clinicians first, then take them to the supervisor; it made every later conversation concrete. Differently: plan alert workflow with nursing leads earlier; the hardest live-mode issues were about who responds and when, not about the model. item.title: Tech news, 15 November 2026: the Fireworks AI breach spreads to Cursor and Uber, phishing follows the Microsoft outage, Check Point's exploited zero-day and SpaceX's AI campuses
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: a leaked Fireworks AI key led to Cursor's breach and exposed Uber driver data, phishing used the Microsoft outage and a Check Point zero-day is exploited.
item.content:encoded:
The Fireworks AI breach is now showing up in its customers' disclosures: Cursor traced its own incident to a key it had given Fireworks, and Uber said driver records held by Fireworks were taken. Attackers used the Microsoft 365 outage as a phishing lure, a Check Point zero-day was exploited to gain root on gateways, and SpaceX announced plans for large AI computing campuses.

Today's brief covers stories from 12 to 14 November.

1. The Fireworks AI breach reaches Cursor and Uber

Cursor said its October breach began with an access key it had issued to Fireworks AI being exposed; the key gave read-only access to a shared storage bucket whose records still contained credentials, which the attacker used to reach some of Cursor's services and plant backdoored extensions1. Separately, Uber said driver records held by Fireworks AI, including driver's licence information, were taken, according to state breach filings2.

CTO take: this is what supply chain risk looks like in AI: one provider's breach becomes many customers' incidents. Never give an AI provider a key with more reach than it needs, never let logs or stored records keep live credentials, and know which of your data each provider holds so you can respond the day they disclose. See AI inference providers are supply chain.

2. Microsoft restores 365 services and warns of outage-themed phishing

Microsoft said Microsoft 365 services were restored for all remaining affected customers after the multi-day disruption, and warned of a phishing campaign exploiting it3. The emails imitated service-health notices, cited a real incident number and pressured recipients to follow fake email recovery links4.

CTO take: every big outage is followed by phishing that uses it. Tell staff that real status information comes from the admin centre or your IT team, never from an email link, and check your mail filters for the reported patterns. See the Microsoft 365 outage playbook.

3. A Check Point zero-day is exploited to take over gateways

CISA added CVE-2026-123039, a privilege escalation flaw in Check Point's Gaia OS, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 13 November6. BleepingComputer reports attackers combined it with other flaws to gain root on gateways through the Mobile Access portal and deploy a wiper aimed at VMware ESXi5.

CTO take: security gateways keep appearing as entry points this year, from Fortinet to Check Point. Apply the vendor's hotfix, disable portals you do not use, check gateways for signs of compromise, and make sure backups of virtualisation hosts are isolated from the networks a compromised gateway can reach. See the management plane hardening case study.

4. SpaceX plans more than $74 billion of AI computing campuses

SpaceX announced plans for AI supercomputing campuses in Arizona and Texas worth more than $74 billion, with the Texas site to generate its own electricity, The Next Web reports7. The plans still depend on local approvals7.

CTO take: new AI capacity is increasingly built with its own power to avoid grid limits and local opposition. For buyers, more capacity is coming, but late and unevenly; plan with several providers and regions. See planning around the AI capacity crunch and the US page.

What I'd do this week

  • Review keys and data you have given AI providers, and remove anything not needed.
  • Warn staff about outage-themed phishing and where real status updates come from.
  • Patch Check Point gateways and disable unused portals.
  • Check that virtualisation backups are isolated from gateway networks.

item.title: AI agents can now pay: what ChatGPT Wallet means for merchants, payment teams and anyone building agents
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: ChatGPT Wallet lets agents buy with approval and tokenised cards. A CTO's take on agent checkout traffic, fraud rules and approval design for merchants and builders.
item.content:encoded:
On 13 November, OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet, letting its agents complete purchases for users with approval each time and tokenised card credentials. Card networks have been building agent payment schemes for months. Agent-initiated checkout is no longer a demo: it is traffic that will reach your store, your fraud rules and your support team. Here is how to prepare, whether you sell online or build agents yourself.

What launched

ChatGPT Wallet lets OpenAI's agents complete purchases for users: people save a card, the agent shows the items, total and card before checkout, and the user approves each purchase; merchants and agents receive tokenised card credentials rather than the real card number1. It is rolling out first to eligible users in the US, and OpenAI plans to support purchases within preset spending limits later2. Cards from Visa, Mastercard and American Express work at launch3.

It lands on rails the card networks have been building: Visa and Mastercard launched agent payment programmes that issue tokens for approved agents and verify them at the network4. Reporting on the launch notes OpenAI warned that some sites may block agent purchases unintentionally and that fraud systems may flag legitimate agent orders2.

How an agent purchase flows

For merchants: four things to decide now

1. Welcome, tolerate or block agents. Bot protection tuned against scrapers will often block agent checkouts too. Decide your policy deliberately. If you want agent sales, learn to recognise verified agents, for example through signed agent requests, rather than opening the door to every bot.

2. Tune fraud rules for a new pattern. Agent orders can look unusual: fast, consistent, from new devices, with tokens rather than typed card details. Review rules that would decline them wholesale, and watch approval rates for agent traffic separately from human traffic.

3. Make product data agent-readable. Agents buy what your data says. Accurate structured data on price, stock, sizes, delivery and returns reduces wrong orders and disputes; see structured data for AI search.

4. Plan for after the sale. Returns, customer service and disputes stay with you. Make sure support can see that an order came through an agent and what the customer approved, so arguments about "I did not mean to buy that" can be resolved.

For anyone building agents that spend money

The approval step is the most important design decision. A good confirmation shows exactly what will happen, in plain terms, inside the conversation, and needs a deliberate action to proceed. MCP's Apps extension shows the pattern for any agent action: an interactive card in the chat that the user confirms5.

An agent that can pay is an agent that can be tricked into paying. Keep a human approval on every purchase until limits, allowlists and monitoring have earned the right to remove it.

Prompt injection matters more once money moves: a product page or email that instructs the agent to buy something is an attack. Treat every page the agent reads as untrusted; see prompt injection defence for agents.

Where this is heading

Expect three things: agent traffic growing first in the US and then elsewhere as networks and wallets expand; pressure to allow purchases within limits without per-transaction approval; and regulators asking who is liable when an agent buys the wrong thing. Payment and consumer protection rules differ widely by market, so merchants selling internationally should watch how each region treats agent-initiated payments. See where I work.

CTO take

For merchants, the cost of preparing is small: a deliberate bot policy, fraud rules reviewed for agent traffic, clean product data and support tooling that shows how an order was made. For agent builders, the hard part is not the payment API but the approval experience and the limits around it. Both groups should start now, while volumes are low enough to learn. item.title: One login bug away: hardening single sign-on, staff access and integration keys for a UK B2B SaaS company
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a UK B2B SaaS company can harden its single sign-on flows, staff support access and integration keys, so one login bug cannot become access to production.
item.content:encoded:
A UK software company sold a collaboration platform to enterprises, most of whom signed in through their own identity providers. Its engineers had built single sign-on support over years, one customer request at a time. Staff could open customer workspaces for support, and integrations held keys to code hosting and the CDN. When another SaaS company disclosed that a flaw in its SSO flow let an attacker pose as staff and reach production, the board asked whether the same chain existed here.

The situation

A UK software company sold a collaboration and documentation platform to mid-sized and large organisations. Most enterprise customers signed in through their own identity providers using SAML or OIDC, and the company had added support for each provider's quirks over several years, in more than one part of the codebase. Support engineers could open any customer workspace to troubleshoot, using the same login system as customers with an internal flag. Integrations with code hosting, the CDN and DNS used long-lived keys, some readable from internal tools staff could reach.

Why now. In November 2026, GitBook disclosed that an attacker used a flaw in its SSO login flow to create sessions as staff, then reached a misconfigured code-hosting integration, internal repositories and a CDN API key that gave production access12. The same week, Apify confirmed that sign-in tokens and two-factor recovery codes had been accessed in an attack3. The UK's voluntary Software Security Code of Practice, published by the government and NCSC, sets expectations for vendors on secure development and on telling customers about incidents45, and enterprise customers had begun asking about it in security reviews.

What had to be true

  • One way in: a single, well-tested authentication path for all SSO, not several.
  • Staff are different: staff access never shares the customer login path.
  • No standing access: support access is granted per case, time-limited and logged.
  • No chains: a staff session cannot reach keys that reach production.
  • Visible: unusual sessions and token use raise alerts.
  • Explainable: if something happens, customers are told quickly what to rotate.

Architecture

All SSO handling moved into one authentication service built on maintained SAML and OIDC libraries, configured strictly: signatures required on assertions, audience and recipient checked, replay prevented and clock skew limited. Provider-specific workarounds became configuration in one place rather than code scattered across the product. Staff signed in through a separate identity provider with hardware security keys; a customer's SSO configuration could never create a staff session.

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: breaking the chain from login to production

Assume the login will be bypassed one day. SSO protocols are intricate and implementation bugs recur across the industry. The design question was therefore not only "is our SSO correct?" but "what can an attacker do with a forged session?". For customer sessions, the answer became: one tenant's data, nothing else. For staff sessions, it became: nothing, until access to a specific workspace is approved, and never the integration keys. The model borrowed from how Kubernetes treats every API request: authenticate, authorise, then apply policy before anything is allowed6.

Integrations with too much reach. The code-hosting integration had been installed with broad permissions years earlier, and CDN and DNS keys could change production routing. Each integration was reinstalled with the minimum permissions it needed, CDN and DNS changes moved to the deployment pipeline with short-lived tokens, and the secrets manager stopped allowing humans to read production secrets at all; only workloads could.

Rotation customers can actually do. GitBook's response asked customers to create new API tokens, rotate integration secrets and review recent changes made by its app1. The company wrote its own version of that notice in advance, listing exactly what customers would need to rotate, and built a one-click way for administrators to revoke all tokens for their workspace.

Every SaaS login flow will have a bug one day. What matters is that a forged session leads nowhere valuable: one tenant at most, never the staff console, never the keys.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Separate staff identity providerStaff flag on customer accountsA customer-side flaw cannot create staff sessions
Just-in-time support accessStanding access to all workspacesLimits what a compromised staff account can see
One central auth serviceFix each SSO code pathOne place to test, review and harden
No human reads of production secretsRestrict to senior engineersRemoves the step from staff session to keys
Minimal integration permissionsKeep broad permissions for convenienceA compromised integration reaches less
Pre-written customer rotation noticeWrite it during an incidentFaster, clearer communication when it matters

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: separate staff access first; it removed the worst-case chain within weeks. Differently: commission an external test of the SSO implementation earlier; it found edge cases in provider-specific handling that internal reviews had missed. item.title: Tech news, 14 November 2026: Nvidia's CEO resigns, ChatGPT Wallet lets agents shop, Apify confirms a breach and the FBI recovers Binance funds
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO, ChatGPT Wallet lets agents buy with approval, Apify confirms a breach and the FBI seizes $1.2B of Binance funds.
item.content:encoded:
Nvidia's chief executive resigned, putting a leadership change at the centre of the AI hardware supply chain. OpenAI gave its agents a way to pay for things with approval each time, an automation platform confirmed customer data was accessed in an attack, and US authorities seized part of last month's record Binance theft.

Today's brief covers stories from 12 to 13 November.

1. Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia's chief executive

Nvidia said Jensen Huang has stepped down as president, chief executive and a board member, effective immediately, and that CFO Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent replacement1. The resignation followed reports about Huang's conduct that Nvidia had been investigating; the board said it expects operations, customer commitments and the product roadmap to continue without interruption12.

CTO take: in the short term, chips already ordered will ship and roadmaps rarely change overnight. Over a year, a leadership change at the dominant AI hardware supplier can shift priorities, pricing and partnerships. This is a good moment to check how dependent your AI plans are on one vendor's hardware and software stack, and whether your serving layer could run on alternatives. See AI capacity contracts.

2. OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet for agent purchases

OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet, which lets its agents complete purchases for users: people save a card, review the items and total, and approve each purchase, while merchants and agents receive tokenised card credentials rather than the real card number3. TechCrunch reports it is rolling out to eligible US users first, and that OpenAI plans to support purchases within preset spending limits later4.

CTO take: agentic commerce is moving from demos to checkouts. If you run an online store, expect agent traffic at checkout: decide whether you will welcome or block it, make sure fraud rules do not reject legitimate agent purchases wholesale, and keep product data structured so agents describe it accurately. If you build agents, keep a human approval step for spending until you have strong limits and monitoring. See agentic infrastructure and the agent-ready marketplace case study.

3. Apify confirms customer data was accessed

Web automation platform Apify confirmed that customer data was accessed in a cyberattack, including salted password hashes, two-factor recovery codes, phone numbers and authentication tokens linked to Google and GitHub sign-ins, with limited card details, SecurityWeek reports5.

CTO take: recovery codes and sign-in tokens are as valuable as passwords. If your teams use Apify, rotate credentials and integration tokens, regenerate two-factor recovery codes and review connected GitHub and Google access. More broadly, list the automation and scraping tools that hold tokens to your code and accounts; they are part of your supply chain. See the third-party access case study.

4. US authorities seize $1.2 billion of the stolen Binance funds

The FBI said US authorities have seized more than $1.2 billion of the cryptocurrency stolen from Binance last month, which it attributes to North Korean hackers known as TraderTraitor, out of more than $2.7 billion frozen with help from crypto firms6. CyberScoop reports authorities also seized infrastructure used in a related social engineering operation7.

CTO take: recovery is welcome but partial; prevention still matters more. For anyone holding digital assets, the lessons from the Binance case remain custody design, withdrawal controls and resistance to social engineering of staff. See custody architecture lessons from the Binance hack.

What I'd do this week

  • Review how dependent your AI roadmap is on one hardware vendor's stack.
  • Decide how your checkout should treat AI agent purchases.
  • Rotate tokens and recovery codes for automation tools that have disclosed breaches.
  • List the third-party tools that hold tokens to your code repositories.

item.title: Microsoft 365 went down: what it broke, why it spread so far, and what to do before the next outage
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: What the November 2026 Microsoft 365 outage broke, why one supplier's failure spread so far, and a practical playbook for surviving the next productivity SaaS outage.
item.content:encoded:
On 12 November 2026, Microsoft 365 failed across regions for much of a working day: email, Teams, SharePoint and Copilot, and for some organisations the security tools that sit on top of them. Your core systems may have been healthy, yet work stopped because the tools people use to communicate, find information and sign in were down. This is what happened, why the impact was so wide, and a playbook for being ready next time, whatever suite you use.

What happened

Problems began with Exchange Online and spread to other Microsoft 365 services and regions on 12 November. Microsoft's advisories listed Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft 365 Copilot and Defender XDR among affected services, and users also reported OneDrive problems13. Microsoft said servers were failing automated health checks and dropping out of service, pushing load onto the rest, and that it had found no indication of malicious activity2. It paused deployments and worked on a configuration change to relieve an overwhelmed connection process3.

The disruption was felt worldwide, with users in Australia reporting problems into the next day4. Recovery was gradual and uneven, and Microsoft has promised a post-incident report with the root cause1. Business customers may be able to claim service credits, but generally need to ask5.

Why one outage reached so far

Most organisations no longer use a productivity suite only for email. Over a few years it has become the place where people talk, store documents, sign in, get AI help and often run security tooling. When it fails, the effects cascade.

The pattern is worth naming: the tools you use to manage an incident are often hosted by the supplier that is having the incident. Many teams discovered that their incident bridge, their contact list and their runbook all lived in Teams and SharePoint.

During an outage: the first hour

Avoid well-meant improvisation: staff forwarding company email to personal accounts, sharing files through unapproved tools or resetting passwords repeatedly. Outages are also a favourite moment for phishing that imitates the supplier's status messages, so warn staff to expect it.

Before the next one: the playbook

1. Map your dependencies. For each critical business process, list what it needs from the suite: email, chat, documents, identity, AI. Most organisations find identity is the biggest single point of failure, because it gates access to everything else.

2. Build an out-of-band channel and use it. Pick a messaging and paging tool from a different provider, with accounts for incident leaders, and use it for routine on-call so it works when needed.

3. Keep critical information outside the suite. Contact lists, escalation paths and top runbooks should exist somewhere that does not depend on it: a separate tool, an offline copy and a short printed card for on-call staff.

4. Plan emergency access. Keep a small number of monitored break-glass accounts that can reach critical systems if the main identity provider is unavailable, protected with hardware keys and tested regularly.

5. Detect independently. Do not rely on the supplier's status page or staff complaints. Simple synthetic checks against sign-in, mail and chat endpoints, run from outside your network, give you earlier warning and your own evidence6.

6. Give customers another route. A status page hosted elsewhere, SMS templates and a phone line mean customers hear from you even when email is down.

7. Decide what AI is allowed to be critical for. If teams rely on an AI assistant for routine work, decide what happens when it is unavailable, and make sure nothing that must happen depends on it alone.

8. Rehearse. Run a short exercise: "the suite is down for a day". It will expose gaps faster than any document review.

You cannot stop a supplier's outage. You can make sure it is an inconvenience rather than a crisis, by deciding in advance how you will talk, decide and serve customers without it.

Should you diversify away from one suite?

OptionBenefitCost
Stay on one suite, add fallbacksSimple, cheap, covers most riskFallbacks must be maintained and used
Separate identity providerSign-in survives a suite outageMore integration and licences
Second suite for critical teamsFull capability during outagesExpensive and confusing day to day

For most organisations, the first option, with careful attention to identity and emergency access, gives the best return. Regulated firms with strict recovery targets may need more; see the Singapore insurer case study and the AI provider resilience case study.

This week

  • Hold a 30-minute review: what stopped, what you improvised, what you would do differently.
  • Record the incident IDs and your impact, and decide whether to claim service credits.
  • Set up an out-of-band channel for incident leaders if you do not have one.
  • Export critical contact lists and runbooks to a location outside the suite.
  • When Microsoft's post-incident report is published, read it and update your plan.

CTO take

This outage was not a security incident, and it will be fixed. Its lasting value is as a free rehearsal: it showed every organisation exactly where it depends on one supplier, at no cost beyond a lost day. Use that evidence now, while people remember it, to fund the small fallbacks that turn the next outage into an inconvenience. item.title: When the suite goes down: keeping a Singapore digital insurer running through a productivity SaaS outage
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a Singapore digital insurer can keep critical services running when its productivity suite fails: dependency maps, recovery targets and fallback channels.
item.content:encoded:
A Singapore digital insurer ran its customer-facing platforms on its own cloud estate, with careful failover. Everything around them, email, chat, documents, identity and increasingly AI assistants, ran on one productivity suite. The insurer had planned for its own systems failing, not for that suite failing. A long outage at a major provider made the gap obvious, and Singapore's business continuity expectations for financial institutions made it urgent.

The situation

A Singapore digital insurer sold travel, health and home policies online. Its policy administration, claims and payments ran on its own cloud estate across two availability zones, with tested failover. Everything else ran on one productivity suite: email, chat, video calls, shared documents, the identity provider staff used to sign in to every other system, and the AI assistant built into it. Customer notices, incident bridges and even the runbooks for failing over the core platform lived there.

MAS's business continuity management guidelines expect financial institutions to identify their critical business services and set, for each, a service recovery time objective: how long it can be disrupted before severe impact, with the recovery times of underlying functions and dependencies fitting inside it23. The insurer had done this for its platforms. It had not traced the dependencies through the productivity suite.

Why now. On 12 November 2026, a long Microsoft 365 outage disrupted Outlook, Exchange Online and Teams for much of a working day; Microsoft attributed it to servers failing health checks and dropping out of service, with no evidence of an attack1. Staff across the industry found they could not email customers, join incident calls or open runbooks. The insurer's board asked a simple question: what would we have done?

What had to be true

  • Dependencies known: each critical service mapped to the SaaS it relies on, identity included.
  • Targets met: workarounds that keep each service within its recovery target.
  • Coordination possible: a way to run an incident without email, chat or shared documents.
  • Customers reachable: notices that do not depend on the failed suite.
  • Access preserved: administrators can reach critical systems if the identity provider is down.
  • Early warning: the insurer knows about an outage before staff start complaining.

Architecture

The first deliverable was a dependency map for each critical business service, built with the people who run them. It showed that the identity provider was the biggest single point of failure: if staff could not sign in, they could not reach the claims system, the cloud console or the paging tool, even though those were healthy.

The data flow, end to end

Detection used the OpenTelemetry Collector's HTTP check receiver, run from small collectors in more than one region, to probe the suite's sign-in, mail and chat endpoints alongside the insurer's own services4. Results went to the observability platform the insurer already used, which did not depend on the suite.

The hard part: identity and the fallback nobody uses

Break-glass without a back door. Emergency accounts that bypass the main identity provider are exactly what attackers want. The insurer kept a small number, each tied to a named role, protected with hardware security keys, stored with sealed procedures, monitored for any use and tested on a schedule. Any use outside an exercise raised an immediate alert to security.

Keeping fallbacks alive. A fallback channel that nobody opens for months will not work when needed: accounts expire, numbers change, people forget. The insurer used the out-of-band messaging tool for real on-call handovers every week, synchronised its contact lists from the HR system daily, and printed a short card of first steps for on-call staff.

Regulatory duties without email. Incident reporting to MAS and notices to customers normally went out by email. The runbook named an alternative route for each, and the compliance team rehearsed it, so a suite outage would not also become a reporting failure.

Resilience plans usually cover your systems failing. The outage that hurts is often the supplier your plan quietly depends on: the one hosting the plan itself.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Fallbacks on different providersBackup features of the same suiteOne outage cannot take out both
Use fallbacks weeklyKeep them for emergencies onlyUnused tools fail when needed
Small, monitored break-glass setNo emergency access, or many accountsAccess when needed without a standing back door
Independent synthetic checksRely on the provider's status pageEarlier warning and your own evidence
Offline runbooks and printed first stepsRunbooks only in shared documentsAvailable when the suite is not
Workarounds sized to recovery targetsGeneric "wait for the provider"Meets MAS expectations per service

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: map dependencies service by service with the people who run them; it surfaced the identity dependency nobody had written down. Differently: include the AI assistant in the map from the start; some teams had begun relying on it for routine customer replies, and its outage was a gap in its own right. item.title: Tech news, 13 November 2026: a long Microsoft 365 outage, EU rules for AI sandboxes, an exploited Xen Orchestra flaw and Nebius's spending plans
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: a long Microsoft 365 outage, EU rules for AI regulatory sandboxes, an exploited Xen Orchestra flaw and Nebius raising capex as AI cloud costs climb.
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft 365 was disrupted for much of a working day, a reminder of how much of most companies runs on one supplier. The EU set common rules for AI regulatory sandboxes, a virtualisation management tool was exploited before many users had patched, and Nebius's results showed how much capital AI cloud capacity now demands.

Today's brief covers stories from 10 to 12 November.

1. Microsoft 365 suffers a long outage

Outlook, Exchange Online, Teams and other Microsoft 365 services were disrupted for much of 12 November; Microsoft said servers failing automated health checks dropped out of service and pushed load onto remaining infrastructure across several regions, and reported no evidence of a cyberattack1. XDA reports Microsoft paused deployments while preparing a configuration change to relieve an overwhelmed connection process2.

CTO take: most companies now depend on one productivity suite for email, chat, files and increasingly AI assistants. You cannot prevent a supplier outage, but you can plan for it: an out-of-band way to reach staff and customers, critical contacts and runbooks available offline, and a clear decision on which processes stop and which continue. Review what broke for you on 12 November while it is fresh. See the supplier resilience case study.

2. The EU sets common rules for AI regulatory sandboxes

The European Commission adopted Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2487, published on 11 November, setting common rules for establishing and running national AI regulatory sandboxes under the AI Act3. EU Law Live reports the rules cover how sandboxes are set up, operated and supervised4; commentary notes participation produces documentation and an exit report rather than any compliance clearance.

CTO take: sandboxes are useful for testing novel AI systems with a regulator watching, especially for smaller companies, but they are not a shortcut to compliance. If you build high-risk AI for the EU, consider a sandbox for genuinely uncertain questions, and keep building your own evidence: risk assessments, evaluations and documentation. See the Europe page and the AI governance programme case study.

3. An exploited Xen Orchestra flaw exposes virtualisation hosts

Vates published advisory VSA-2026-062 on 10 November for an actively exploited authentication bypass in Xen Orchestra that lets attackers gain administrative access and take over XCP-ng hosts; SC Media reports exploitation leaves little trace in Xen Orchestra's own logs5.

CTO take: management consoles for virtualisation, backup and networking are the keys to everything beneath them, and many teams that moved to open-source hypervisors run them with less scrutiny than their old platforms. Patch to the fixed versions in the advisory, keep management interfaces off the internet and behind strong access controls, and check hosts for signs of compromise. See the management plane hardening case study.

4. Nebius raises spending plans as AI cloud capacity gets costlier

Nebius reported third-quarter results on 11 November and its shares fell the next day; it raised its 2026 capital spending forecast and guided 2026 revenue to the low end of its range, Investing.com reports6.

CTO take: specialist AI clouds are spending heavily ahead of revenue. For buyers, that can mean good prices today and more uncertainty later. Diversify across providers, prefer contracts that let you move, and watch the financial health of any provider you rely on for production capacity. See AI capacity contracts.

What I'd do this week

  • Hold a short review of how the Microsoft 365 outage affected you and what you would do differently.
  • Patch Xen Orchestra and confirm management consoles are not internet-facing.
  • Decide whether any EU AI work would benefit from a regulatory sandbox.
  • Check the financial outlook of AI cloud providers you depend on.
